title: Pages versus journeys: choosing the sample
description: A page-by-page sample tests whether every template conforms. A journey-based sample tests whether someone can actually finish the thing they came to do — and most of the barriers that block a task live in states that don't have their own URL.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a page-inventory sample from a journey-based sample and what each actually tests
Select critical user journeys for a scope based on task value rather than ease of testing

contentSections.title: Why a page-by-page sample misses the barrier that actually blocks someone

contentSections.body: A retailer audit tests the homepage, a product page, and the cart page individually — each one passes a full manual check, no critical findings. Nobody tested the actual sequence a shopper follows: land on a product, add to cart, apply a promo code, continue as guest, enter payment. The promo code field's error state is announced only as a colour change; a screen reader user who mistypes the code gets no indication anything failed, and the disabled 'Continue' button gives no reason why. Every page in isolation was fine. The journey wasn't.

contentSections.scenario: Two testers each get 20 hours on the same retail site. Tester A tests 15 individual page templates end-to-end for WCAG conformance, one at a time. Tester B walks 5 complete user journeys — account creation, primary purchase, order lookup, returns, and support contact — start to finish through every step each one requires.
contentSections.question: Which approach is more likely to find the barrier that actually stops someone finishing a task?

options.label: Tester A — 15 templates is more total surface area than 5 journeys
Tester B — most task-blocking barriers live in states a page inventory never visits
Both find the same barriers, just organised differently

feedback.pages: More templates covered is real, but it's coverage of the wrong unit. A validation error, a disabled-button state, a modal that only opens mid-flow, a confirmation screen reachable only after three prior steps — none of these have their own page in a site map, so a page-by-page plan never tests them at all.
feedback.journeys: Right. A page inventory answers 'does every template conform on its own.' A journey answers 'can someone actually do the thing' — and it forces the tester through every transitional state (a loading spinner, an inline error, a step change) in the order a real user actually hits it, which is exactly where task-blocking barriers tend to live.
feedback.same: They genuinely aren't organising the same coverage differently — a page inventory structurally cannot reach a state that only exists between two pages, no matter how many templates it includes.

contentSections.concept: **A barrier that blocks a task usually lives in a state, not a page.** Modals, inline validation, step transitions and confirmation screens are the places carts get abandoned and forms get given up on — and a scope built entirely from a site's page list will test every one of those templates in isolation while never once walking the sequence that actually produces the state where the barrier lives.

contentSections.body: In practice this doesn't mean throwing out the page inventory. You can't test literally everything in a fixed number of hours, so the honest move is choosing 4–8 critical journeys that represent what people actually come to do — not what happens to sit at the top of the site map. Good sources for this: analytics on the most common entry-to-conversion paths, support tickets tagged with an accessibility complaint, and whatever the business itself would call its most consequential flow (the one that makes money, or the one a regulator will ask about).

Page templates still earn a place in the scope, just a different one. A unique component pattern — a custom-built dropdown, a data table, a modal, a carousel — should get isolated component-level testing on top of the journeys, because a defect in a shared component shows up everywhere that component is reused, not only inside the specific journeys chosen to walk it. A well-built scope is usually journeys (to catch full-task barriers) layered with a component inventory (to catch pattern-level defects), not one or the other.
A page inventory tests whether templates conform. A journey tests whether the task can be finished — and most of what actually blocks someone lives in a state a page list never visits.

contentSections.title: Picking journeys that matter, not journeys that are easy to test

contentSections.body: A scope proposal lists three journeys: 'View homepage. View About page. View Contact page.' Each is a single click, quick to document, and none is something a user comes to the site to accomplish — nobody's actual goal is 'look at the About page.'

contentSections.scenario: The auditor picked those three because the site map made them the fastest things to click through and write up, not because a stakeholder or any usage data pointed at them as what users are trying to do.
contentSections.question: What's the actual failure driving this scope choice?

options.label: The auditor doesn't understand what a journey is
Scope was chosen by convenience — what's fast to test — instead of by task value — what a user is actually trying to accomplish
The site genuinely doesn't have any real journeys worth testing

feedback.confused: The proposal does technically list multi-step-looking items, so it isn't a definitional mix-up — the actual problem is what drove the selection, not whether the auditor knows the word.
feedback.convenience: Right. Every real site has at least one thing people actually come to do — buy something, register, look something up, file a complaint — and none of those three items is it. They were chosen because they're quick, not because they matter.
feedback.no-journeys: Every site with any functional purpose has at least one real task a user is trying to complete — even a static informational site usually has a 'find the information I need and act on it' path worth testing. 'No real journeys exist' is very rarely actually true.

contentSections.mechanism: **Scope drifts toward whatever's easiest to click through unless something actively anchors it to what users are actually trying to do.** The fix is sourcing journeys from evidence outside the auditor's own convenience: analytics on the top entry-to-exit paths, support tickets tagged 'couldn't complete' or 'accessibility,' and a direct conversation with the client about what actually makes the product money or fulfils its purpose. If a client already has a known accessibility complaint, testing that exact journey belongs in scope by default — the whole audit's credibility rests on whether it catches the thing the client already knows is broken.

contentSections.body: A journey worth testing is one a real user is trying to accomplish, sourced from analytics, complaints, or business priority — not whatever's fastest to click through and write up.

title: Representative sampling of a large site
description: On a site built from a handful of templates, random sampling mostly retests the same pattern by chance. A sample stratified by template plus deliberate outlier-hunting is what actually guarantees every distinct pattern gets seen.

learningObjectives.text: Build a stratified sample by template rather than a random page sample on a large, template-driven site
Identify hand-built, one-off pages a template-based sample structurally cannot surface

contentSections.title: A thousand pages, twenty hours: what actually gets sampled

contentSections.body: A university's site has roughly 4,000 pages, built from six templates — news article, faculty profile, course listing, event page, department homepage, generic content page — plus a shared component library. A scope proposal says 'we will test 40 representative pages.'

contentSections.scenario: Two competing sampling proposals for the 40 pages. Proposal A: 40 pages selected by a random number generator across all 4,000. Proposal B: 2–3 pages per template (12–18 pages) plus every page identifiably built outside the six templates — an embedded PDF viewer page, an interactive campus map page.
contentSections.question: Which is actually representative of the site's real coverage risk?

options.label: Proposal A — true randomness is the only unbiased way to sample
Proposal B — stratified by template plus explicit outliers guarantees every distinct pattern is seen at least once
They're equivalent at 40 pages either way

feedback.random: Randomness sounds unbiased, but on a site built from six templates it mostly means re-drawing the same handful of patterns by chance — with 4,000 pages split across six templates unevenly, a small template with only 30 instances can easily draw zero pages in a 40-page random sample, leaving that entire pattern untested.
feedback.stratified: Right. Guaranteeing 2–3 instances of every template means every distinct pattern gets tested at least once, and content-driven variance within a template (an article with a table versus one without) gets a chance to surface too. The outlier pages catch exactly what a template list can't: anything built once, outside the pattern, by hand.
feedback.equivalent: They aren't equivalent — random sampling has a real, non-trivial chance of missing an entire smaller template outright, which stratified sampling by construction cannot do.

contentSections.concept: **Representative doesn't mean random on a template-driven site — it means guaranteed coverage of every distinct pattern.** A site built from a small number of templates has almost all of its real accessibility risk concentrated in those templates, not in which specific instance of each one gets drawn. Stratifying by template and forcing a minimum count per template converts 'probably covered, if we're lucky' into 'definitely covered.'

contentSections.body: The rough arithmetic that produces a defensible number: for each of the N templates, budget 2–3 instances (enough to catch template-level defects and some real content variance, like an article that happens to embed a video versus one that doesn't) plus every page that uses a pattern found nowhere else — a page with an embedded PDF viewer, an interactive map, a third-party payment widget. Testing meaningfully more pages beyond that mostly re-tests the same six patterns again, at diminishing return for the hours spent.
On a template-driven site, representative means stratified by template plus deliberate outliers — not random, which can miss an entire pattern by chance.

contentSections.title: The outlier that isn't on any template list

contentSections.body: Content teams sometimes hand-build one-off pages outside the CMS's normal templates — a campaign landing page for a fundraising push, a page embedding a third-party donation widget, a microsite built once for a single event and never touched again. None of these show up on a template inventory, because by definition they aren't built from one.

contentSections.question: If your sample is built entirely from a list of CMS templates, what's the one category of page it will systematically miss, no matter how many pages you test?
contentSections.answer: Hand-built, one-off pages that exist outside the CMS's normal templates — a campaign microsite, an embedded third-party widget, anything built once by hand rather than generated from a template — because they simply don't appear on any template inventory. Finding them requires either an actual site crawl or asking content owners directly, not counting instances of known templates.
contentSections.hint: A template inventory can only list things that are, by definition, instances of a template — think about what category of page structurally cannot be one.

contentSections.body: Two practical ways to find these before the sample is finalised: a real crawl of the live site (a crawler tool will surface every URL that actually exists, template or not — worth naming its cost if the client hasn't budgeted for one, since some crawlers are free for small sites and paid at scale) and directly asking content owners 'which page took the most custom work to build.' That question tends to surface exactly the page most likely to have been hand-coded outside the normal pattern, and least likely to have ever been tested by anyone.
A template inventory can only ever list instances of templates — the page built once, by hand, outside the pattern needs a crawl or a conversation with content owners to find at all.

title: Choosing the test matrix: browsers, tech, platforms
description: A naive matrix of every screen reader times every browser times every OS runs past a hundred combinations nobody can afford. A defensible matrix is built from real usage data and the client's actual product, not from trying to cover everything.

learningObjectives.text: Build a test matrix from real assistive-technology usage data rather than arbitrary completism
Adjust a default test matrix to match a specific client's actual platform and technology stack

contentSections.title: 144 combinations, one audit: why you can't test everything

contentSections.body: A first-draft test matrix lists 4 screen readers, times 4 browsers, times 3 operating systems, times 2 device types — 96 theoretical combinations before keyboard-only, voice control, and switch access are even added in. No audit anyone can afford tests 96 combinations.

contentSections.scenario: The client's users are, per the client's own analytics, almost entirely Windows and macOS desktop users plus a smaller iOS mobile share, in the US.
contentSections.question: Of that huge combinatorial list, how many specific combinations realistically need to be in the matrix to cover the overwhelming majority of how real assistive-tech users actually access this product?
contentSections.explanation: Something close to 4 — NVDA+Chrome (the single most common desktop screen reader/browser pairing in survey data going back years), JAWS+Chrome (the other dominant desktop pairing), VoiceOver+Safari on macOS, and VoiceOver+Safari on iOS (VoiceOver ships with every Apple device and is, in practice, the only screen reader most iOS users have ever used — there's essentially no meaningful market of third-party screen readers on iOS the way there is on Windows). Add keyboard-only testing across the primary browser as a fifth line that isn't a screen reader at all. That's the matrix that actually reflects this specific client's userbase — not 96 theoretical cells, most of which represent combinations almost nobody is using.

contentSections.body: The usage data worth citing directly in a scope document: WebAIM's periodic screen reader survey, which has consistently shown NVDA and JAWS dominating desktop usage (often with NVDA ahead, both usually paired most often with Chrome), and VoiceOver's effective monopoly on Apple platforms. Where a client has their own analytics on browser and OS share among their actual users, that data should override generic survey numbers — a client whose users skew heavily to Firefox for some specific reason (an enterprise IT policy, a regional preference) needs Firefox pairings the generic survey wouldn't flag as a priority.
A defensible matrix is built from real usage data — a screen reader survey, the client's own analytics — not from trying to multiply out every theoretical combination.

contentSections.title: The client's own tech stack changes the matrix

contentSections.body: A client's product is a native iOS app used inside hospitals, with no desktop product at all. A default desktop-heavy matrix — NVDA+Chrome, JAWS+Chrome — would spend most of the audit's hours testing a platform this product doesn't run on, while under-testing VoiceOver, Voice Control, and Switch Control on the one platform patients and staff actually use.

contentSections.scenario: The client's mobile-only banking app is available on both iOS and Android, US-based users, no desktop or tablet-only version exists.
contentSections.question: Which of these belong in this client's test matrix? Select all that apply.

items.label: VoiceOver on iOS Safari/the app's native views
Voice Control on iOS (real, documented use among users with motor disabilities for banking-app navigation)
TalkBack on Android, since the app also ships there

explanation.voiceover-ios: Yes — this is the primary screen-reader path for the platform the product actually runs on.
explanation.voice-control-ios: Yes — voice control is a real, documented access method for people with motor disabilities interacting with mobile apps, and a banking app's forms and confirmations are exactly the kind of interaction worth testing this way.
explanation.talkback-android: Yes — the app ships on Android too, so its screen reader deserves the same coverage iOS gets, not an assumption that 'we already tested VoiceOver so Android is probably fine.'
explanation.jaws-windows: No — there is no desktop product for JAWS to run against. Budgeting hours here tests a platform this product doesn't exist on.
explanation.nvdaff: No, for the same reason — no desktop surface exists for NVDA to encounter.

contentSections.synthesis: The matrix follows the product, not a generic default list. A mobile-only product's matrix should be almost entirely mobile assistive technologies — testing desktop screen readers against a product with no desktop presence spends real hours on combinations that literally cannot occur for a real user, at the direct expense of hours that could go toward the platform this specific product actually runs on.

contentSections.body: The scope document should state the matrix's rationale explicitly and tie it to a source — 'per WebAIM's latest survey' or 'per the client's own analytics showing X% Safari, Y% Chrome' or 'the product has no desktop surface, so desktop AT is out of scope' — rather than presenting a fixed default list as if it applies to every client identically. A matrix without a stated rationale reads as arbitrary the moment someone asks why a particular combination was or wasn't included, and a client is entitled to ask.
The matrix follows the product's actual platforms and the client's actual usage data — a generic default list applied unchanged to every client wastes hours on combinations nobody uses.

title: Scoping to fit the hours you actually have
description: Twenty hours against four hundred screens has no version that covers everything at real depth. The honest move is prioritising by risk and traffic, disclosing what wasn't covered, and building the effort estimate from real per-unit time costs instead of hoping it fits.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate competing ways to allocate a fixed audit budget and identify which produces the most useful result
Estimate the hours a journey or component realistically costs to test to a defensible depth

contentSections.title: 20 hours, 400 screens: the honest trade-off

contentSections.body: A client has budgeted 20 hours for a WCAG audit of a product with roughly 400 unique screens. There is no version of 20 hours that covers 400 screens at genuine manual-testing depth — the arithmetic simply doesn't work, and the scope document has to decide honestly what happens instead.

contentSections.scenario: Three ways to spend the fixed 20 hours. Option A: run automated scanning tools across all 400 screens, no manual testing at all. Option B: pick the highest-risk, highest-traffic journeys and components and test those at genuine manual depth, leaving the rest explicitly untested and disclosed. Option C: split the 20 hours evenly across all 400 screens, giving each a few minutes of moderate-depth attention.
contentSections.question: Which produces the most useful audit for the hours actually available?

options.label: Option A — full automated coverage of everything is better than manual coverage of a fraction
Option B — deep manual testing on the highest-risk journeys, with the rest explicitly disclosed as untested
Option C — spreading the hours evenly gives every screen at least some attention

feedback.automated: Automated tools reliably catch a real but limited slice of WCAG issues — commonly cited estimates put it around 20–40% of what a manual audit would find — because they can't evaluate things like whether alt text is meaningful, whether a keyboard trap exists, or whether an ARIA pattern is used correctly for its actual context. Running automated-only across everything produces the appearance of full coverage while missing most of the defects that actually block someone, and reporting it without that caveat would misrepresent what was actually verified.
feedback.prioritised: Right. Automated tools catch a real but limited slice of what's wrong — commonly cited figures put manual-equivalent coverage around 20–40% — so 'we scanned everything' quietly overstates what was actually verified. Deep, real manual testing on the journeys most likely to matter, paired with an honest, explicit list of what wasn't covered, gives the client something they can actually act on and doesn't imply false completeness.
feedback.even: A rushed, shallow pass across everything is likely to miss exactly the defects that require actually completing an interaction to find — a focus trap in a multi-step form, a live region that fails only on the second submission, a dynamic reorder that only breaks tab order under a specific condition. These need real depth to surface, and spreading the hours evenly guarantees nobody gets it.

contentSections.concept: **A fixed hour budget is a real constraint, not a problem to hide from the client.** The professional response to 'not enough hours to cover everything' is prioritising by risk and traffic and disclosing exactly what wasn't covered — not quietly running a shallow or automated-only pass across the full surface and letting the client believe that means everything was checked.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to the exclusions work in this module's final lesson: disclosing what wasn't covered isn't a weakness in the scope, it's the thing that makes the rest of it trustworthy. A client who later discovers a barrier in a screen the audit never claimed to cover has a very different reaction than one who discovers it in a screen the audit implied was checked.
A fixed budget doesn't stretch to cover everything at depth — prioritising by risk and disclosing what's left out produces a more useful audit than a shallow or automated-only pass across everything.

contentSections.title: Effort estimate: what a page or a journey actually costs in hours

contentSections.body: A five-step registration wizard with client-side validation needs testing with more than one assistive technology, and every finding needs evidence captured and written up — the raw testing time is only part of what the hours line in a scope document actually needs to cover.

contentSections.scenario: Testing that five-step wizard thoroughly means: a keyboard-only pass through all five steps, one full pass with NVDA+Chrome, one full pass with VoiceOver+Safari, capturing evidence at every defect found, and writing up the findings afterward.
contentSections.question: Realistically, how many hours should this one journey get budgeted, evidence and write-up included?
contentSections.explanation: Something in the region of 3 hours for a journey of this complexity is a reasonable working estimate: roughly 20–30 minutes for the keyboard-only pass, 30–45 minutes per assistive-technology pass (two passes here), and write-up/evidence time that experienced auditors commonly budget as roughly equal to or more than the raw testing time, since a finding that isn't documented to reproduction standard is functionally not a finding yet. A simple single-page content check might cost 20–30 minutes total; a multi-step interactive journey across two ATs realistically costs an order of magnitude more.

contentSections.body: These rough per-unit figures — 20–30 minutes for a simple content page, several hours for a complex multi-step interactive journey tested across more than one AT — are what turn a scope document's hours line from a guess into arithmetic: (journeys × their individual estimate) + (component instances × their estimate) + a buffer for write-up and report assembly. A scope that states '20 hours' with no visible math behind it is much easier to dispute later than one that shows its work.
The hours line in a scope document should be arithmetic built from real per-unit time costs, not a round number picked to sound reasonable.

title: Writing exclusions the client agrees to in advance
description: Silence in a scope document reads as inclusion, not exclusion. What's genuinely out of scope has to be named explicitly and confirmed in writing before testing starts, or it becomes a dispute after the report is delivered.

learningObjectives.text: Write an explicit exclusions list rather than relying on silence to communicate what's out of scope
Explain why written sign-off on a scope document matters more than verbal agreement

contentSections.title: What 'out of scope' actually needs to say

contentSections.body: Three weeks after an audit report is delivered, a client pushes back: 'why didn't you test our PDF downloads?' The original scope document never mentioned PDFs at all — not included, not excluded, just absent — and the client assumed that silence meant they were covered.

contentSections.scenario: The scope document listed what was in scope in detail but said nothing at all about document accessibility, native apps, or third-party embedded content — it simply didn't come up.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind this dispute?

options.label: The client is being unreasonable — they should have asked if they were unsure
Absence gets read as inclusion — a scope document silent on something reads to a client as 'everything else is covered,' so genuinely out-of-scope items need to be named explicitly, not just left out
PDFs are always out of scope for accessibility audits by industry default, so this shouldn't need stating

feedback.unreasonable: This shifts responsibility onto the client for a document that never actually told them anything one way or the other — a scope document exists precisely so the client doesn't have to guess or ask.
feedback.silence: Right. A client reading an 'in scope' list naturally assumes anything not explicitly excluded is either included or simply wasn't relevant — they have no way to distinguish 'we forgot to mention this' from 'we deliberately excluded this' unless the document tells them which one it is.
feedback.default: There's no universal industry default here — some audits do include document accessibility, some don't, and a client working with a new auditor has no way to know which convention this particular audit followed without being told directly.

contentSections.mechanism: **A positive, explicit exclusions list is what closes the gap silence leaves open.** It isn't enough to describe what's in scope and stop — anything a client might reasonably expect to be covered but genuinely isn't needs its own line, stated plainly, precisely because the alternative (just not mentioning it) reads as an oversight or as coverage, never as a deliberate boundary.

contentSections.body: Categories worth naming explicitly whenever they're genuinely excluded: third-party embedded content outside the client's own control (a payment iframe from an external vendor, an embedded chat widget, a third-party analytics consent banner), document accessibility (PDFs, Word documents) if it's a separate deliverable or genuinely out of scope, native mobile apps if only the web product was scoped, any environment not actually tested (staging vs. production, a specific region's version of the site), and content still under development or explicitly marked 'coming soon.'
Anything a client might reasonably expect to be covered but genuinely isn't needs its own explicit line in the scope — silence reads as coverage, never as a boundary.

contentSections.title: Getting sign-off before day one, not after the invoice

contentSections.body: A scope document is emailed to a client on a Friday. Testing starts the following Monday, before any reply comes back. Two weeks later, when a stakeholder disputes what was and wasn't covered, there's no record of anyone at the client's side actually having agreed to the document testing was run against.

contentSections.question: Does a verbal 'sounds good' over a call count as scope sign-off?
contentSections.answer: No — it needs a written, dated confirmation of the specific scope document version, not a verbal agreement. A phone call leaves no record of exactly what was agreed, or when, or against which version of the document — and when a 'why wasn't X tested' dispute comes up weeks later, an email reply confirming the scope doc is the artefact that actually resolves it. Verbal agreement resolves nothing once memories of the call diverge.
contentSections.hint: Think about what specifically gets disputed later, and what kind of record would actually settle that dispute — a memory of a call, or a dated document.

contentSections.body: In practice this doesn't need to be a formal contract amendment — a simple email reply confirming 'yes, this scope document is what we're testing against' is enough, as long as it's in writing, dated, and references the specific version of the document being agreed to. It's worth keeping that confirmation on file for the life of the engagement, and treating any material change discovered mid-audit (the site turns out to be three times the size the client described, or a journey they said was simple turns out to have five sub-flows) as a trigger to revisit the scope explicitly with the client, rather than silently absorbing the extra work or silently dropping coverage to stay within the original hours.
A scope document only functions as a defence against later disputes if there's a written, dated record of the client actually agreeing to it — a verbal 'sounds good' leaves nothing to point back to.

title: Practice — Scope Seven Audits Under Different Constraints
description: Seven drills across the module's skills, each dropping you into a different real-world scoping constraint. No new concepts: this is where scoping a real audit stops being something you've read about and becomes something you can do fast under pressure.

learningObjectives.text: Apply journey selection, sampling, matrix-building, budget-fitting and exclusion-writing to unfamiliar constraints at speed
Distinguish a well-justified scoping decision from one made purely for convenience

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or split across a few — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write a Full Audit Scope for a Real Product
description: Pick a real product you can access today and write the scope document you'd actually hand a client: sample, matrix, method, exclusions, and an effort estimate that shows its arithmetic.

learningObjectives.text: Map a real product's critical journeys and build a representative sample from them
Build a defensible test matrix tied to real usage data for a specific product
Write an explicit exclusions list and an hours estimate a client could actually sign off on

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a real product you can access today — a retailer, a bank, a government service, a SaaS tool you already use. This lab produces a real scope document for it: the kind you'd actually send a client before testing starts, not a summary of what you'd theoretically do.

contentSections.title: Write a full audit scope for a real product
contentSections.brief: Choose a real product (web-based, at least a few distinct page templates and one multi-step journey) you can access with the energy you have today. Produce a scope document covering: the sample (journeys and templates), the test matrix (with a stated rationale), the method, an explicit exclusions list, and an effort estimate that shows its arithmetic.
contentSections.deliverable: A scope document with sample, matrix, method, exclusions and effort estimate — specific enough that a client could read it and know exactly what will and won't be tested, and sign off on it.

stages.title: Choose the product and map its journeys
stages.instructions: Pick a real product. List its 6–10 page/screen templates. Then name 3–5 critical user journeys — the things a real user actually comes to do — sourced from what you can observe about the product's purpose (not from what's structurally easiest to click through).
stages.checkpoint: You have a named product, a short template list, and 3–5 named journeys with a one-line reason each was chosen.

stages.title: Build the sample and the test matrix
stages.instructions: From the templates, select 2–3 representative instances each, plus any outlier page you notice that doesn't fit a template. Then build a test matrix: which assistive technologies and browser/platform combinations, and why — tie the rationale to real usage data (a screen reader survey, or the product's own likely userbase) rather than a generic default list.
stages.checkpoint: The sample lists specific pages/instances per template plus any outliers, and the matrix has a stated rationale for every combination included.

stages.title: Write the exclusions list and the effort estimate
stages.instructions: Write an explicit exclusions list naming anything a client might reasonably assume was covered but genuinely isn't (third-party embeds, document accessibility, other platforms). Then build the effort estimate: a per-journey/per-template time figure, summed to a total, with a write-up buffer added.
stages.checkpoint: Exclusions are named specifically, not implied by silence. The effort estimate shows its arithmetic, not just a final number.

stages.title: Self-check against the rubric
stages.instructions: Read the full document once as if you were the client receiving it cold. Run the self-check below before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: Every rubric criterion below is met, or you've noted specifically what's still missing.

rubric.criterion: The sample is built from journeys and stratified templates, not a page-by-page or random selection
rubric.meets: A reader can see which journeys were chosen and why, and which templates the page sample covers, with any outliers named separately.

rubric.criterion: The test matrix has a stated rationale tied to real usage data
rubric.meets: Every AT/browser/platform combination in the matrix is justified by a named source — a survey, the product's known userbase, or a stated platform constraint — not left unexplained.

rubric.criterion: The exclusions list is explicit, not implied by silence
rubric.meets: At least one thing a client could reasonably assume was covered is named and explicitly marked out of scope, with a reason.

rubric.criterion: The effort estimate shows real arithmetic
rubric.meets: The final hours figure is visibly built from per-item estimates summed together, with a write-up buffer added, not a single unexplained number.

rubric.criterion: The document reflects a real energy budget
rubric.meets: The four stages were completed as separate sittings if needed — nothing about writing this scope required doing it in one unbroken 50-minute block.

contentSections.body: A scope document you've never actually written for a real product is a scope process you've only read about — this lab is the difference between knowing the pieces and having produced the thing a client would actually sign.

title: Checkpoint — Scoping an Audit
description: Ten questions on this module. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core scoping distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Scoping an Audit
contentSections.framing: This is the first module in this phase, so every question pulls from here. That changes from the next module on.

questions.prompt: A page-by-page sample tested three pages individually and found nothing. A real user still got stuck between two of them. What did the sample most likely miss?

options.label: A transitional state — a modal, an inline error, a step change — that only exists mid-journey and has no page of its own
Nothing — if all three pages passed, the journey between them must also be fine
The pages weren't tested thoroughly enough individually

questions.explanation: A barrier that blocks a task usually lives in a state, not a page — a modal, a validation error, a step transition. A page-by-page sample never visits these because they don't have their own URL.

questions.prompt: A site is built from 6 templates across 4,000 pages. Why is a stratified sample (2–3 instances per template plus outliers) more representative than a random sample of the same size?

options.label: Random sampling can, by chance, miss an entire smaller template outright; stratified sampling structurally guarantees every template is seen
Random sampling is always biased toward whichever template has the most pages
They're equally representative at any sample size

questions.explanation: Stratifying by template guarantees coverage of every distinct pattern; a random draw across all 4,000 pages has a real, non-trivial chance of drawing zero pages from a smaller template.

questions.prompt: What kind of page does a template-based sample structurally fail to catch, no matter how many template instances are tested?

options.label: A hand-built, one-off page that exists outside the CMS's normal templates — a campaign microsite, an embedded widget built once
The homepage, since it's usually excluded from templates
Pages with unusually long text content

questions.explanation: A template inventory can only ever list instances of templates. Pages built once, by hand, outside the pattern need a crawl or a conversation with content owners to find at all.

questions.prompt: Why is 'JAWS on Windows × 4 browsers × VoiceOver nowhere' a bad matrix for a product that supports both Windows and macOS?

options.label: It's exhaustive on one axis (browsers) while missing an entire real platform (macOS/VoiceOver) that the product actually supports
JAWS should never be tested against more than one browser
Nothing is wrong with it — more browser pairings is always better

questions.explanation: Multiplying out browsers exhaustively for one platform while leaving out VoiceOver entirely means an entire supported platform gets zero coverage, despite the matrix looking thorough by cell count.

questions.prompt: With a fixed, tight hour budget against a large product, which produces the most useful audit?

options.label: Deep manual testing of the highest-risk, highest-traffic journeys, with what's left explicitly disclosed as untested
An automated-only scan across everything, since it technically touches every page
Splitting the hours evenly and thinly across everything

questions.explanation: Automated tools catch a real but limited slice of issues (commonly estimated around 20-40% of what manual testing finds); prioritised deep testing with honest disclosure of what wasn't covered is more useful than shallow or automated-only coverage of everything.

questions.prompt: A scope document never mentions PDF accessibility at all. Weeks later the client asks why PDFs weren't tested. What went wrong?

options.label: Silence was read as inclusion — anything not explicitly excluded reads to a client as covered, so genuine exclusions need their own explicit line
Nothing went wrong — PDFs are always out of scope for accessibility audits by default
The client should have specifically asked about PDFs before signing off

questions.explanation: A scope document silent on something reads as coverage, not as a boundary — anything a client might reasonably expect to be included needs an explicit exclusion line if it genuinely isn't.

questions.prompt: Why does a verbal 'sounds good' over a call not count as real scope sign-off?

options.label: It leaves no dated record of exactly what was agreed, against which version of the document — an email confirmation is what actually resolves a later dispute
Verbal agreements are never legally binding for any purpose
It's fine as long as more than one person heard the call

questions.explanation: A written, dated confirmation referencing the specific scope document is the artefact that actually resolves a 'why wasn't X tested' dispute later — a memory of a call resolves nothing once accounts diverge.

questions.prompt: A client's usage data shows heavy Firefox use due to an internal IT policy, even though general survey data favours Chrome. What should the test matrix do?

options.label: Include Firefox pairings based on the client's own specific data, overriding what the generic survey alone would suggest
Ignore the client's data and follow the generic survey exactly, since it's the industry standard
Test only Firefox, since that's what the client actually uses

questions.explanation: Client-specific, verifiable usage data should override generic survey defaults when it's available — the survey describes typical usage, and this client's usage isn't typical.

questions.prompt: What should an hours estimate for a complex multi-step journey, tested across two assistive technologies, actually include beyond raw testing time?

options.label: Evidence capture and write-up time, which experienced auditors commonly budget as roughly equal to or more than the raw testing time
Nothing extra — the estimate should reflect only the time spent actively operating the assistive technology
A flat doubling of whatever number feels reasonable

questions.explanation: A finding that isn't documented to reproduction standard is functionally not a finding yet — write-up and evidence-capture time is real, necessary time that belongs in the estimate, not an afterthought.

questions.prompt: A client's site turns out to be three times larger than described after the scope was agreed and testing has already started. What's the correct response?

options.label: Flag the discrepancy to the client directly and explicitly revisit the scope together — adjusting hours, sample, or both
Silently absorb the extra work without telling the client
Silently test less than originally promised and say nothing

questions.explanation: A material change to the scoped facts should go back through the same explicit-agreement process as the original scope — silently absorbing or silently under-delivering both avoid the conversation the discrepancy actually calls for.

contentSections.body: None of these need to be perfect. What matters is which ones needed a guess — that's what the next checkpoint will bring back.

title: Reproduction steps for a screen reader finding
description: A finding a developer can't reproduce is a finding that sits in the backlog untouched — exact repro steps, not a description of the symptom, are what actually get a bug fixed.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a vague symptom description from actionable, exact reproduction steps
Write reproduction steps precise enough for a developer with no assistive technology experience to follow

contentSections.title: The finding that sits in the backlog for six months

contentSections.body: A finding reads: 'The search field doesn't announce properly with a screen reader.' No browser named. No operating system. No screen reader named, let alone a version. No steps. Six months later it's still open — not because nobody cares, but because nobody who picked it up could get it to happen.

contentSections.scenario: Two versions of the same finding. Version A: 'Search field doesn't announce properly with a screen reader.' Version B: 'On nvda.org's NVDA 2024.4 with Chrome 131 on Windows 11: load the homepage fresh, press Tab 4 times to reach the Search input, type "shoes," press Enter. Expected: NVDA announces "142 results for shoes." Actual: NVDA announces nothing — the results count is never read.'
contentSections.question: Which version is actually a finding a developer can act on without you in the room?

options.label: Version A — it correctly identifies that something is wrong with the search field and a screen reader
Version B — it names the exact software, exact steps, and exact expected versus actual behaviour
Both are equally usable — the developer can figure out the details themselves

feedback.a: Version A identifies that a problem exists, but a developer with no screen reader experience has no starting point — which of a dozen screen readers, which browser, which exact interaction, what should have happened versus what actually happened. That gap is exactly what leaves a finding unreproduced.
feedback.b: Right. Every variable a developer would otherwise have to guess is stated: the specific AT and version, the specific browser and OS, the exact keystrokes from a defined starting point, and precisely what was expected against what actually happened. Nothing here requires the developer to already know how to operate a screen reader.
feedback.both: The gap between them is the entire reason one finding gets fixed and the other sits open for months — 'figure it out themselves' means a developer with no AT background has to first learn to operate a screen reader just to attempt reproduction, which most teams simply never get around to.

contentSections.concept: **A finding a developer can't reproduce is, functionally, not a finding yet — it's a lead.** The gap between 'something's wrong with the search field' and a step-by-step reproduction is the entire difference between a bug that gets fixed this sprint and one that gets closed as 'couldn't reproduce' after someone spends twenty minutes clicking around without a screen reader running at all.

contentSections.body: The reason this matters more for screen reader findings specifically than most other bug types: most developers on most teams have never operated a screen reader and don't know the keyboard commands to navigate one, let alone how to interpret what it announces. A repro step like 'navigate to the search field and search' assumes fluency the reader doesn't have. 'Press Tab 4 times from page load, type your query, press Enter' assumes nothing beyond being able to press keys — which is exactly the level of assumption a repro step should be pitched at.

The starting state matters as much as the steps themselves. 'Tab 4 times' only reaches the search field reliably if the page was just freshly loaded — if a cookie banner appeared and was dismissed first, or if a previous search already changed the page's focusable elements, the tab count changes and the steps silently stop working for the next person who tries them. Always state the starting condition explicitly: 'from a fresh page load, logged out' is a real starting state; 'navigate to the page' is not.

A finding a developer can't reproduce is a lead, not a finding — exact software versions, exact steps from a defined starting state, and exact expected-versus-actual behaviour are what turn one into the other.

contentSections.title: Writing steps someone with no assistive-tech experience can actually follow

contentSections.body: A repro step reads: 'Use the screen reader to navigate to the error message.' A developer with no screen reader experience has no idea what command that even means — 'navigate to' isn't a keystroke, and 'the error message' isn't a landmark they know how to reach.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order that actually makes reproduction steps usable by someone unfamiliar with assistive technology.
steps: State the exact starting point (URL, logged-in state, fresh load vs. mid-flow)
State the exact assistive technology, version, browser and OS being used
List the exact keystrokes or gestures in order, one action per line
State exactly what was expected to happen at the relevant step
State exactly what actually happened, in the screen reader's own words where possible
contentSections.explanation: Each step removes one specific way a developer without AT experience gets stuck. Without the starting point, the same keystroke sequence lands somewhere different depending on where the page already was. Without the exact software and version, a keystroke that works in one screen reader does nothing in another. Without keystroke-by-keystroke steps, 'navigate to X' asks the reader to already know how — the exact thing they don't. And the expected-versus-actual pair is what turns 'something sounds off' into a specific, falsifiable claim a fix can be checked against afterward.

contentSections.body: Where possible, quote the screen reader's actual announcement rather than paraphrasing it — 'NVDA announces nothing' is a real, checkable claim; 'NVDA doesn't say the right thing' isn't, because 'right' was never defined. The next lesson covers capturing that announcement precisely, but the repro steps themselves should already be written assuming the exact wording matters, not just the general gist.
Reproduction steps should assume the reader can press keys and nothing else — every screen reader command, every starting condition, and every exact announcement spelled out rather than assumed.

title: Screenshots, recordings and announcement transcripts
description: A screenshot that doesn't show where keyboard focus actually is proves nothing about a keyboard finding, and 'the screen reader said something wrong' isn't evidence until the exact words are transcribed.

learningObjectives.text: Capture a screenshot or recording that actually proves a keyboard or focus-related finding
Transcribe a screen reader announcement verbatim rather than paraphrasing it

contentSections.title: The screenshot that doesn't actually prove anything

contentSections.body: A finding about a missing focus indicator is submitted with a screenshot of the page. The screenshot shows the button in question, styled normally, with no visible focus ring anywhere on the page — because the tester took the screenshot after tabbing away to switch to the screenshot tool, and focus had already moved off the element entirely.

contentSections.code:
Evidence-capture process, as actually followed:
1. Tab to the element being tested
2. Confirm (by eye) that no visible focus indicator appears
3. Press the OS screenshot shortcut (which requires switching input focus to the screenshot tool)
4. Attach the resulting screenshot to the finding
contentSections.question: This process has a real flaw that undermines the exact thing it's trying to prove. What is it?

options.label: Nothing is wrong — the screenshot shows the page in the state described
Step 3 breaks the very thing being evidenced: switching to the screenshot tool moves keyboard focus away from the element before the capture happens
The screenshot should be in a different file format

feedback.nothing: The screenshot technically shows the page, but it can't show what it needs to — the absence of a focus indicator that was, by the time of capture, no longer even the element's problem to display, since focus had already moved elsewhere.
feedback.focus-moves: Right. A standard OS screenshot shortcut requires switching input focus to trigger it, which is exactly the action that moves keyboard focus off the element under test. The resulting screenshot proves nothing about whether a focus indicator was visible while the element actually held focus — it can't, because it wasn't taken at that moment.
feedback.format: File format has nothing to do with whether the screenshot's content is actually valid evidence of the claim being made.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A screen recording, rather than a still screenshot, sidesteps this problem entirely — the tab key press and the resulting (or absent) focus indicator both appear in the same continuous capture, with nothing needing to switch away mid-sequence. Where a still image is genuinely preferable (a report that needs to show a single frame clearly), a delayed-capture screenshot tool (one that starts a countdown before switching focus to capture) or a capture triggered by a hotkey that doesn't require switching window focus solves the same problem.

contentSections.body: A screenshot can only prove a keyboard-state claim if it's captured without disturbing the keyboard state it's trying to prove — a screen recording, or a delayed/hotkey capture method, is usually the safer default.

contentSections.title: What the screen reader actually said, in its own words

contentSections.body: A finding says 'NVDA announces the error message incorrectly.' What NVDA actually said was 'Edit, blank, invalid entry' with no indication of which field or what the actual error was — but 'incorrectly' is the only word that made it into the write-up, and a developer reading it has no way to know what 'correctly' would even sound like.

contentSections.question: Why does an exact, verbatim transcript of a screen reader's announcement matter more than a general description like 'the announcement was unclear'?
contentSections.answer: Because 'unclear' is a judgement, not a checkable fact — a developer can't verify a fix against 'make it clearer.' The verbatim announcement ('Edit, blank, invalid entry') is a specific, reproducible claim: exactly what was said, in what order, with what actually missing (which field, what the error is). A fix can be checked directly against that transcript afterward — did the new announcement actually include the missing information — in a way 'make it clearer' can never be verified against.
contentSections.hint: Think about what a developer would need in hand to confirm, after making a change, that the problem is actually fixed.

contentSections.body: Most screen readers offer a way to capture exactly what was spoken, not just what was seen on screen: NVDA's Speech Viewer window shows a running text log of every announcement, which can be copied verbatim; VoiceOver's caption panel (enabled in VoiceOver Utility) does the same on macOS and iOS. Recording the screen with one of these visible — or narrating aloud what's heard, if the tool isn't available — turns 'it sounded wrong' into an exact transcript a developer can compare their fix's output against, word for word.
A vague description of an announcement can't be verified against a fix. A verbatim transcript — captured with a speech viewer or caption panel, not remembered afterward — can.

title: Recording the environment: version, platform, settings
description: The same bug can reproduce on one screen reader version and not the next, and settings most testers never think to record — verbosity, punctuation level, browser zoom — can independently change whether a finding shows up at all.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an exact assistive-technology version can change whether a finding reproduces
Identify the non-obvious settings that can independently affect reproduction of a finding

contentSections.title: The bug that was already fixed in the version the developer has

contentSections.body: A finding reads: 'NVDA doesn't announce the error correctly.' The developer, who happens to have the latest NVDA installed, tries to reproduce it and can't — the error announces fine. The finding gets closed as 'couldn't reproduce.' The auditor's version was NVDA 2023.1; the developer's was 2024.4, six releases later, in which an unrelated NVDA bug affecting exactly this kind of error announcement had, by coincidence, already been fixed upstream.

contentSections.scenario: Neither the finding nor the developer's reproduction attempt was dishonest — both were accurate for the specific NVDA version each person had installed.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind the two people getting different, both-true results?

options.label: The developer wasn't testing carefully enough
Screen readers are actively developed software with their own bug fixes and regressions between versions — the exact version matters because behaviour genuinely differs release to release
This kind of discrepancy is rare enough not to be worth documenting versions for

feedback.carelessness: Nothing points to carelessness — the developer's result was accurate for their exact NVDA version, just as the auditor's was for theirs. Blaming the person misses that the software itself changed between the two attempts.
feedback.version: Right. NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver and every other screen reader are actively maintained software, shipping their own bug fixes and occasional regressions on a real release schedule. A finding tied to a specific version is a claim about that version — not a permanent fact about the product — and needs the version stated for anyone to know whether their own environment should even be expected to reproduce it.
feedback.rare: This exact kind of discrepancy is common enough that omitting the version is one of the most frequent reasons a real finding gets wrongly closed as unreproducible — it isn't a rare edge case, it's routine.

contentSections.mechanism: **A finding without a stated software version is a claim with an unstated scope.** 'NVDA doesn't announce X' silently means 'the NVDA version I happened to have installed on the day I tested this' — which might be six releases and a year of bug fixes away from whatever version the developer, or a later retester, actually has. Naming the exact version turns an ambiguous claim into a specific, checkable one, and tells a developer whose environment differs that a mismatch is expected, not a sign the finding was wrong.

contentSections.body: This cuts both ways worth naming honestly in a finding: a bug that reproduces on an older AT version but not a newer one might mean it's already been fixed upstream (worth verifying and closing, or downgrading in urgency) — or it might mean the newer version happens to sidestep this one interaction pattern while the underlying markup issue is still real and will resurface the next time the AT vendor changes something else. Naming the version precisely is what lets whoever picks this up next make that judgement instead of guessing at it.
Screen readers are actively developed software — a finding without an exact version number is a claim about an unstated, possibly-already-changed target.

contentSections.title: The settings nobody thinks to write down

contentSections.body: Two testers report opposite results on the same page: one says a form field's instructions are announced, the other says they aren't. Both are right — one had NVDA's verbosity set to 'speak object descriptions' on, the other had it off, and the instructions were only exposed through a description field NVDA reads at one verbosity level and skips at another.

contentSections.scenario: Deciding which environment details are worth recording alongside every finding, beyond the AT name and version already covered.
contentSections.question: Which of these settings can genuinely change whether a finding reproduces? Select all that apply.

items.label: Screen reader verbosity level (e.g. NVDA's 'speak object descriptions,' punctuation level)
Browser zoom/text-size level, since layout and reflow behaviour can change at different zoom levels
OS-level high-contrast or forced-colours mode, which can change how custom-styled elements render or disappear entirely
The desktop wallpaper visible before the browser was opened
How many other tabs happened to be open in the browser at the time

explanation.verbosity: Yes — verbosity settings directly control which content a screen reader announces at all, as the hook shows. Two testers with different verbosity settings can get genuinely different, both-accurate results from the identical page.
explanation.browser-zoom: Yes — zoom level changes reflow, and reflow can expose or hide content, change tab order visually (though not in the DOM), or trigger responsive breakpoints that behave differently, all of which can change whether a finding is visible.
explanation.high-contrast: Yes — forced-colours modes override custom CSS colours and can make a custom-styled control (a checkbox built from divs rather than a native input, for instance) render invisibly or unrecognisably, independent of any screen reader setting at all.
explanation.desktop-wallpaper: No — this has no mechanism by which it could affect page rendering, screen reader announcement, or any tested behaviour.
explanation.browser-history: No — background tabs with no active interaction have no mechanism to affect the tested page's rendering or announcement behaviour either.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the ones that matter: each is a setting that changes what content actually gets exposed or rendered — through the accessibility tree, through CSS, through layout — not a setting that merely describes the environment cosmetically. Anything that can plausibly change what's exposed to the user belongs in the recorded environment; anything that's purely incidental to the desktop doesn't.

contentSections.body: In practice this doesn't mean recording every possible setting for every finding — it means being alert to which settings are plausibly relevant to the specific finding at hand, and stating them explicitly whenever there's a real chance they matter (any finding involving custom-styled controls should note whether forced-colours mode was tested; any finding involving verbosity-dependent content should state the verbosity level used).
Verbosity, zoom, and forced-colours settings can each independently change whether a finding reproduces — record whichever ones are plausibly relevant to the specific thing being tested.

title: The finding that only reproduces sometimes
description: An intermittent finding is tempting to drop because it doesn't fit a clean, binary repro step — but a bug that fails 30% of the time is a real bug with a real pattern, and the pattern itself is the evidence.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether an intermittently-reproducing finding is worth reporting and how to document it honestly
Diagnose the likely mechanism (usually timing) behind a finding that fails only sometimes

contentSections.title: The bug that works fine seven times out of ten

contentSections.body: Submitting a form triggers a live-region success message. Testing it ten times: seven times NVDA announces 'Form submitted successfully.' Three times, nothing is announced at all — the same form, the same steps, no visible difference in what was clicked. It's tempting to write this off as unreliable and drop it.

contentSections.scenario: An auditor considers three responses to the 30%-failure pattern: drop the finding entirely as 'not reliably reproducible'; report it as a normal finding with no mention of the intermittency; report it with the observed pattern and frequency stated explicitly.
contentSections.question: Which is the right call?

options.label: Drop it — a finding that doesn't reproduce reliably every time isn't solid enough to report
Report it normally with no mention of the intermittency, to avoid making it sound less serious than it is
Report it with the observed frequency and pattern stated explicitly — for example, roughly 3 in 10 attempts

feedback.drop: A user hitting this 30% of the time is a real user experience, not a testing artefact — dropping it because it isn't binary throws away a genuine, frequent barrier for no good reason.
feedback.hide: Reporting it as if it fails every time overstates the claim in a different direction — a developer trying to reproduce it 'every time' and getting it to work 7 times in a row might reasonably conclude the finding is wrong, which is the same 'couldn't reproduce, closing it' outcome as dropping it entirely.
feedback.report-honest: Right. A 30% failure rate is a real, frequent problem for real users, and stating the observed frequency honestly is both accurate and more useful to a developer than either extreme — it tells them what to expect when they try to reproduce it themselves, and signals that a race condition or timing issue is worth investigating rather than a markup error that would fail consistently.

contentSections.concept: **An intermittent finding is still a real finding — the pattern of when it fails is itself the evidence.** Findings that fail some but not all of the time are usually pointing at a timing-dependent mechanism: a live region updated before the browser has finished registering the DOM change, a race between an API response and a focus move, an announcement that gets interrupted by another one firing close behind it. None of that makes the bug less real for the fraction of users who hit it — it just means the honest report states the observed pattern rather than forcing it into a false binary.

contentSections.body: A finding that reproduces some but not all of the time is still real — the honest move is stating the observed frequency and pattern, not dropping it or reporting it as if it always fails.

contentSections.title: Documenting a pattern, not just a percentage

contentSections.body: Testing the same 30%-failure finding more carefully across another ten attempts turns up something specific: it fails every time the form is submitted within about a second of the page finishing load, and succeeds every time there's a longer pause first. 'Fails 30% of the time' becomes something a developer can actually investigate.

contentSections.problem: Document the intermittent live-region finding from this pod's hook so a developer has an actual investigative lead, not just a failure percentage.

steps.label: Note the raw pattern observed across repeated attempts
steps.work: 10 attempts submitting immediately after page load: 7 failures, 3 successes. 10 attempts with a 3+ second pause before submitting: 0 failures.
steps.why: Recording the raw counts, not just a summary percentage, gives a developer something to try to reproduce with a specific procedure, not a vague ratio.

steps.label: State the likely mechanism as a hypothesis, not a certainty
steps.work: Likely a race condition: the live region's ARIA attributes may not be fully registered by the browser's accessibility tree before the DOM update fires, if submission happens before the page has finished its own initial setup.
steps.why: Naming a plausible mechanism (without overclaiming certainty — 'likely,' not 'is') gives the developer a specific, testable place to start looking, rather than a fix-in-the-dark bug report.

steps.label: State the reliable reproduction condition found
steps.work: Submitting within ~1 second of page load reliably fails; submitting after a 3+ second pause reliably succeeds.
steps.why: This is the actual, non-obvious lead — a condition that flips the bug from rare to near-certain, which is far more useful than 'it happens sometimes.'

faded.problem: A separate finding: a 'Save draft' autosave confirmation announces correctly most of the time, but fails specifically when the user has been typing continuously for more than 30 seconds without pausing.

blanks.prompt: What raw pattern should be recorded, beyond a summary percentage?
blanks.answer: The specific counts from repeated attempts under both conditions — e.g. how many failures out of how many attempts when typing continuously past 30 seconds, versus when pausing periodically.
accept: raw failure/success counts under each condition
blanks.why: A developer needs something they can actually try to replicate step by step, not just an aggregate number.

blanks.prompt: What's a reasonable hypothesis to state about the mechanism, without overclaiming certainty?
blanks.answer: Possibly a debounce or throttling mechanism on the autosave/announcement logic that behaves differently under sustained continuous input versus intermittent input — worth investigating, not asserted as fact.
accept: a plausible, hedged guess at the technical cause, not stated as certain
blanks.why: A hedged, plausible mechanism gives the developer a starting point to investigate without the auditor overstating what they actually know about the codebase.

blanks.prompt: What's the actual reliable reproduction condition to state explicitly?
blanks.answer: Typing continuously for 30+ seconds without pausing reliably triggers the failure; pausing periodically reliably avoids it.
accept: the specific condition that flips the bug from rare to consistent
blanks.why: This is the single most useful sentence in the whole write-up — it turns an unreliable-seeming bug into something a developer can trigger on demand.

contentSections.procedure: For any intermittently-reproducing finding: record raw counts under repeated attempts, look for a condition that correlates with failure (timing, input speed, network delay, page load state), state a hedged hypothesis about the mechanism, and — if found — state the specific condition that makes it reliably reproduce, since that's the single most actionable thing in the whole write-up.

contentSections.body: Look for the condition that correlates with failure — timing, load state, input speed. Finding it turns 'happens sometimes' into a reliable, investigable repro step.

title: Keeping evidence organised across a long audit
description: Two hundred findings and three weeks in, a screenshot named 'Screenshot 2026-03-04 at 14.22.11.png' is functionally lost — a naming convention and finding-ID system set up before testing starts is what keeps evidence findable when the report actually gets written.

learningObjectives.text: Design a naming and folder convention that keeps evidence traceable back to specific findings across a long audit
Sequence the steps of setting up an evidence system before testing begins, not partway through

contentSections.title: Two hundred findings, one folder called 'screenshots'

contentSections.body: Three weeks into a large audit, report writing begins. The evidence folder contains 340 files, most named by the OS default — 'Screenshot 2026-03-04 at 14.22.11.png,' 'Screen Recording 2026-03-06 at 09.41.02.mov.' Which finding each file actually belongs to is, at this point, mostly a guess.

contentSections.intro: Design a file-naming convention that would have prevented this. Build it field by field.

fields.prompt: What should come first in the filename, so a file can be matched to its finding at a glance?
options: A sequential finding ID, e.g. F-014
fields.correctValue: A sequential finding ID, e.g. F-014

feedback.A sequential finding ID, e.g. F-014: Right — this is the one piece of information that directly links the file back to a specific line in the findings tracker, which is the whole point.
feedback.The date and time only: A timestamp tells you when a file was created, not which finding it belongs to — exactly the problem in the hook.
feedback.A random unique code: A random code is unique but meaningless on sight; someone still has to look it up somewhere to know what it refers to.

fields.prompt: What should come next, to make the file identifiable without opening it?
options: A short, specific description of what the file shows, e.g. checkout-payment-focus-trap
fields.correctValue: A short, specific description of what the file shows, e.g. checkout-payment-focus-trap

feedback.A short, specific description of what th: Right — this lets anyone scanning a folder of file names understand roughly what each one is without opening every single one.
feedback.Nothing further is needed: An ID alone is enough to trace the file back to its finding, but a folder of 340 files named only by ID is still hard to scan visually for a specific topic.
feedback.The tester's initials: Useful in some team contexts, but it doesn't help identify what the evidence actually shows, which is the more common need when scanning.

fields.prompt: What should come last, to distinguish this file from other evidence of the same finding?
options: The AT/browser combination used, e.g. nvda-chrome
Nothing — one file per finding is always enough
A version number with no other context
fields.correctValue: The AT/browser combination used, e.g. nvda-chrome

feedback.The AT/browser combination used, e.g. nv: Right — a single finding often has multiple evidence files (a screenshot and a recording, or evidence from two AT combinations per the matrix), and this distinguishes them at a glance.
feedback.Nothing — one file per finding is always: Many findings genuinely need more than one piece of evidence — a repro on two different AT combinations, or a screenshot plus a recording — and a naming scheme needs to handle that.
feedback.A version number with no other context: A version number alone doesn't communicate anything about what makes this file different from a sibling file for the same finding.

contentSections.synthesis: Put together: F-014_checkout-payment-focus-trap_nvda-chrome.png. Anyone scanning the evidence folder can see, without opening a single file, which finding it belongs to, roughly what it shows, and which environment it was captured in — the exact three things '340 auto-named files' made impossible to know at a glance.

contentSections.body: A useful evidence filename answers three questions at a glance: which finding, what it shows, and in what environment — an OS default filename answers none of them.

contentSections.title: Setting the system up before day one, not partway through

contentSections.body: Retrofitting a naming convention onto 340 already-captured files, after the fact, at the start of report writing, costs real hours that setting the system up on day one would have avoided entirely — and some of the context needed to rename them correctly (which finding this actually was) is, by that point, already lost.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order you'd actually take to set up an evidence system, before testing starts.
steps: Decide and document the finding-ID scheme and evidence filename convention
Create the folder structure evidence will be captured into
Set up a findings tracker (spreadsheet or tool) with one row reserved per finding ID as findings are discovered
Capture evidence during testing, named and filed according to the convention immediately, not batched for later
Cross-check periodically during the audit that every tracker row has its evidence files present and correctly named
contentSections.explanation: This order front-loads the decisions that are cheap to make before any evidence exists and expensive to retrofit afterward. The convention and folder structure need to exist before the first file is captured, or the first batch of evidence is already inconsistent with whatever gets decided later. Naming and filing immediately during testing — not 'I'll organise this at the end' — is what prevents the exact pile-up in this lesson's hook, since the context needed to name a file correctly is freshest the moment it's captured. The periodic cross-check catches drift early, while there's still time to fix a mis-filed item, rather than discovering the gap only once report writing has already begun.

contentSections.body: None of this needs to be elaborate — a shared folder with subfolders per finding ID, or a flat folder with the naming convention doing all the organising work, both work fine. What matters is that the decision gets made once, before testing starts, and gets followed consistently for every finding captured after that, rather than being invented halfway through or reconstructed from memory at the end.
The evidence system is cheapest to set up before the first file exists and most expensive to retrofit after the last one does — decide it on day one and follow it every time.

title: Practice — Write Reproduction Steps for Eight Findings
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where writing evidence a developer can act on stops being something you've read about and becomes something you do fast, by habit.

learningObjectives.text: Apply reproduction-step writing, evidence capture and environment recording to unfamiliar findings at speed
Distinguish evidence that's genuinely actionable from evidence that only looks thorough

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or a few at a time — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Evidence a Full Set of Findings to Developer Standard
description: Find a set of real findings on a real product and build a complete evidence pack for them: repro steps, captured evidence, recorded environment, and an organisation system a developer could actually navigate without you in the room.

learningObjectives.text: Write reproduction steps precise enough for someone unfamiliar with assistive technology to follow
Capture screenshots, recordings and verbatim announcement transcripts that actually prove a finding
Organise a multi-finding evidence pack with a consistent, traceable naming system

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a real product you can access today — the same one from the previous module's scoping lab works well, or any other. This lab produces a small, real evidence pack: not a description of findings, but the actual repro steps, captured evidence, and organisation a developer would receive.

contentSections.title: Evidence a full set of findings to developer standard
contentSections.brief: Find at least 4 real accessibility findings on a real product (screen reader, keyboard, or both). For each, produce full reproduction steps, captured evidence (screenshot, recording, or transcript as appropriate), and recorded environment details. Organise the full set with a consistent naming and tracking system.
contentSections.deliverable: An evidence pack a developer could reproduce every finding from without needing to ask you a single clarifying question.

stages.title: Find findings and write reproduction steps
stages.instructions: Test a real product (keyboard and/or a screen reader) and find at least 4 genuine findings. For each, write full reproduction steps: exact environment, exact starting state, exact keystrokes/gestures, exact expected-versus-actual.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least 4 findings, each with repro steps someone unfamiliar with the AT used could follow exactly.

stages.title: Capture evidence for each finding
stages.instructions: For each finding, capture appropriate evidence: a screenshot or recording that doesn't require disturbing the state being evidenced, and — for any screen reader finding — a verbatim transcript of the actual announcement (or its absence) using a speech viewer, caption panel, or careful narration.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has at least one piece of captured evidence, and any announcement claim is backed by an exact transcript, not a paraphrase.

stages.title: Record the environment for each finding
stages.instructions: For each finding, record the specific software versions used, and any settings plausibly relevant to that specific finding (verbosity, zoom, forced-colours, or others as applicable).
