If any finding seemed intermittent, note the observed pattern honestly rather than treating it as purely binary.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding states its exact environment, and any intermittent behaviour is documented as a pattern rather than dropped or overstated.

stages.title: Organise and self-check
stages.instructions: Assign each finding an ID and apply a consistent naming convention across all evidence files. Build a simple tracker (even a short list) linking each ID to its finding and evidence. Then run the self-check below.
stages.checkpoint: Every rubric criterion below is met, or you've noted specifically what's still missing.

rubric.criterion: Reproduction steps assume no prior assistive-technology experience
rubric.meets: A reader who has never used the specific AT could follow the exact steps and reach the same result, with the starting state stated explicitly.

rubric.criterion: Evidence proves the claim rather than merely illustrating it
rubric.meets: Screenshots/recordings don't require an action that disturbs the state being evidenced, and any announcement claim has a verbatim transcript.

rubric.criterion: The environment is recorded precisely for every finding
rubric.meets: Exact software versions are stated, plus any settings plausibly relevant to that specific finding.

rubric.criterion: Any intermittent finding is documented honestly
rubric.meets: If applicable, the observed pattern and frequency are stated explicitly rather than the finding being dropped or forced into a false binary.

rubric.criterion: The evidence set is organised and traceable
rubric.meets: Every finding has a consistent ID, and every evidence file's name ties back to that ID at a glance.

contentSections.body: An evidence pack you've never actually assembled for real findings is a process you've only read about — this lab is the difference between knowing what good evidence looks like and having produced it.

title: Checkpoint — Evidence That Holds Up
description: Ten questions on this module. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core evidence-capture distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Evidence That Holds Up
contentSections.framing: Still early in this phase, so every question pulls from this module.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: A finding says 'search doesn't announce properly.' What's missing that would actually let a developer reproduce it?

options.label: The exact AT/browser/OS, exact steps from a stated starting point, and exact expected-versus-actual behaviour
Nothing — a developer can figure out the specifics themselves
A severity rating

questions.explanation: A finding a developer can't reproduce is functionally a lead, not a finding — the exact software, exact steps from a defined starting state, and exact expected-versus-actual close that gap.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: Why does stating the starting state ('fresh page load, logged out') matter as much as the tab count in a repro step?

options.label: The same tab count only reaches the same element reliably from the same starting point — from anywhere else, it lands somewhere different
It doesn't matter — a correct tab count works from any starting point
It only matters for mobile testing

questions.explanation: A tab count is only meaningful relative to a specific starting point — without stating it, a correct count can silently stop working for the next person who tries the steps from a different state.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: A screenshot taken by switching to a screenshot tool (which requires a focus switch) is submitted as evidence of a missing focus indicator. What's the problem?

options.label: The act of switching to capture the screenshot moves keyboard focus off the element, so the screenshot can't actually show whether the indicator was visible while focus was there
Nothing — screenshots are always valid evidence regardless of how they're captured
The screenshot should have been a different file format

questions.explanation: A standard screenshot shortcut requires a focus switch that disturbs the exact state being evidenced — a screen recording or delayed-capture method avoids this.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: Why is a verbatim transcript of a screen reader's announcement better evidence than a description like 'the announcement was unclear'?

options.label: The exact transcript is a specific, checkable claim a fix can be verified against; 'unclear' is a judgement that can't be checked
Transcripts are required by WCAG for all findings
There's no real difference — both communicate the same thing

questions.explanation: A verbatim transcript is a checkable fact a developer can compare their fix's output against directly; a vague description of impression can't be verified either way.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: A finding reproduces on NVDA 2023.1 but a developer with NVDA 2024.4 can't reproduce it. What's the most likely explanation, and what should have prevented the confusion?

options.label: Screen readers change between releases; stating the exact version tested in the original finding would have let the developer recognise a version mismatch instead of assuming the finding was wrong
The developer must not have tested carefully
This kind of discrepancy is rare and not worth planning for

questions.explanation: Screen readers are actively developed software with real behaviour changes between versions — an unstated version turns a specific, explainable mismatch into an apparent contradiction.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: A finding involves whether a form field's instructions are announced. What setting should be recorded alongside it, and why?

options.label: Screen reader verbosity level — it directly controls whether that kind of content gets announced at all
The desktop wallpaper in use
How many browser tabs were open

questions.explanation: Verbosity settings directly control what content gets announced — two testers with different verbosity settings can get genuinely different, both-accurate results from an identical page.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: A live-region announcement fails about 30% of the time and succeeds the rest. What's the right way to handle this finding?

options.label: Report it with the observed pattern and frequency stated explicitly, rather than dropping it or presenting it as purely binary
Drop it, since a finding that isn't consistently reproducible isn't solid enough to report
Report it as if it fails every time, to make sure it's taken seriously

questions.explanation: A real user hitting a barrier 30% of the time experiences a real, frequent problem — the honest and most useful move is stating the actual observed pattern, not forcing it to a false binary or discarding it.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: What's the single most useful thing to find and state when documenting an intermittent finding, beyond the raw failure percentage?

options.label: A specific condition that correlates with failure — e.g. timing, input speed, or page-load state — that makes the bug reliably reproducible
The name of the person who first noticed the inconsistency
A guarantee that the bug will be fixed by a specific sprint

questions.explanation: Finding the condition that correlates with failure turns 'happens sometimes' into a reliable, investigable repro step — often the single most actionable sentence in the write-up.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: A filename reads 'F-014_checkout-payment-focus-trap_nvda-chrome.png.' What three things does this convention communicate at a glance?

options.label: Which finding it belongs to, roughly what it shows, and which environment it was captured in
Only the date the screenshot was taken
Only which tester captured it

questions.explanation: A useful evidence filename answers which finding, what it shows, and in what environment — an OS-default filename answers none of these.

questions.from: This module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: A large audit is a week in with no naming convention yet in place. What's the right move?

options.label: Start the convention immediately for everything going forward, and rename the first week's files now while the context is still fresh
Keep using default filenames for consistency, since switching partway through would look inconsistent
Wait until the audit ends and rename everything at once

questions.explanation: Continuing an unusable system to preserve consistency trades a small, temporary problem for a much larger one — starting immediately and renaming the backlog while memory is fresh costs far less than reconstructing it later.

contentSections.body: None of these need to be perfect. What matters is which ones needed a guess — that's what the next checkpoint will bring back.

title: Impact, frequency, and whether there's a workaround
description: Severity isn't a single number pulled from intuition — it's the combination of how badly a finding affects someone, how often they'd actually hit it, and whether there's a real way around it once they do.

learningObjectives.text: Rate a finding's severity using impact, frequency and workaround as explicit, separate inputs
Identify when a low-impact finding is actually high-severity because of high frequency or no workaround

contentSections.title: Three separate questions, not one gut feeling

contentSections.body: Two findings sit side by side in a draft report. Finding one: a decorative icon has a redundant, slightly verbose alt text ('icon of a star icon'). Finding two: the 'Submit application' button on a five-minute job application form has no accessible name at all — a screen reader announces only 'button,' with no way to tell it apart from the three other unlabelled buttons on the same page. Both are technically WCAG failures. Rating them the same severity would be a mistake almost anyone would notice immediately — but naming exactly why is the actual skill.

contentSections.scenario: A severity framework built from three separate questions: Impact (does this block the task entirely, or just add friction?), Frequency (how often would a real user actually encounter this?), Workaround (is there a real way to get around it, or is the user simply stuck?).
contentSections.question: Applying this to the 'Submit application' button with no accessible name — what does it score on each axis?

options.label: Low impact, low frequency, has a workaround
High impact (blocks task completion), high frequency (every screen reader user hits the submit button), no workaround
It can't be scored without knowing the exact WCAG success criterion it violates

feedback.low: This significantly understates it — every single screen reader user attempting the application has to click something, and with four unlabelled buttons on the page, submitting confidently (rather than guessing) is genuinely blocked.
feedback.high: Right. Impact is high because the task — completing and submitting the application — cannot be confidently finished at all. Frequency is high because every screen reader user who reaches this form hits this exact button. And there's no workaround: nothing on the page tells them which of the four unlabelled buttons is the right one.
feedback.needs-criterion: The WCAG criterion (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value, most likely) matters for the citation, but severity is a judgement about real-world impact, frequency and workaround — not something the criterion number itself determines.

contentSections.concept: **Severity is impact, frequency and workaround, rated as three separate questions, not one intuitive number.** A finding can be technically minor by conformance-checklist standards and still be high severity because it's hit by everyone, blocks the task, and has no way around it — or technically serious-sounding and genuinely low severity because almost nobody encounters it and an easy alternative path exists.

contentSections.body: Applying the same three questions to the redundant alt text: impact is low (mildly annoying repetition, but the icon's meaning is still conveyed and nothing is blocked), frequency is potentially high (every screen reader user passing this icon hears it), but the presence of a workaround is almost beside the point when impact is already this low — the finding is real, worth fixing, and legitimately a much lower priority than the submit button, even though 'redundant text' and 'no accessible name' can both get filed under the same broad WCAG principle.

The workaround question deserves its own scrutiny, because a workaround that only works for some users, or that itself requires knowledge a first-time user wouldn't have, doesn't really count as one. 'The user can figure out which button is Submit by trial and error' is not a workaround in any meaningful sense on a form that submits something consequential — accidentally clicking the wrong unlabelled button next to it might trigger 'Save as draft' or 'Cancel,' and there's no way to know without already knowing the answer.

Rate impact, frequency, and workaround as three separate, explicit questions — a finding that scores low on the WCAG-checklist-severity-implied-by-the-criterion-number can still be the highest-priority thing in the whole report.

contentSections.title: When a 'minor' finding is actually severe because of frequency

contentSections.body: A single low-contrast label appears once, on one rarely-visited settings page, affecting perhaps a handful of users a month. A different low-contrast label appears on every single product card across an entire e-commerce catalogue — the exact same visual defect, but one instance versus thousands of exposures a day.

contentSections.scenario: Two auditors rate these two low-contrast findings identically, reasoning that they're 'the same bug' with the same fix (raise the contrast ratio).
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that should separate their severity ratings?

options.label: Nothing should separate them — identical defects should always get identical ratings

Frequency of exposure is a genuine, independent input to severity — the same defect encountered by thousands of users daily is a bigger real-world problem than one encountered rarely, even though the fix and the underlying cause are identical
The product-card version should actually be rated lower, since it's easier to fix at scale via a shared style

feedback.identical: This treats severity as a property of the defect alone, but severity is about real-world impact on real users — the same defect at wildly different exposure scales genuinely produces a different amount of real-world harm.
feedback.frequency: Right. Frequency is one of the three explicit inputs from this lesson's first pod, and it operates independently of how similar or even identical two defects are technically. The product-card version affects vastly more people, vastly more often — that's a real difference in severity, not just in how widespread the fix needs to be.
feedback.easier-lower: How easy something is to fix is a completely separate question from how severe it is — an easy fix for a high-severity, high-frequency problem is still a high-severity finding; ease of fixing affects prioritisation of effort, not the severity rating itself.

contentSections.mechanism: **The same underlying defect can carry a different severity rating depending on how many real people encounter it and how often.** This is exactly why root-cause grouping (covered later in this module) doesn't mean 'group everything with the same fix into one severity' — it means naming the shared cause while still rating (or at least noting) the real exposure difference, since a defect hit by everyone using the site daily deserves to be flagged with that frequency explicitly, not folded silently into a rating that assumes it's rare.

contentSections.body: Frequency of exposure is a real, independent input to severity — an identical technical defect can be a minor finding in one place and a major one in another, purely because of how many real people hit it.

title: The blocker: nobody using this tech can finish the task
description: 'Critical' or 'Blocker' severity has a precise meaning worth defending precisely: complete task failure for an entire category of assistive-technology user, not just an especially annoying finding.

learningObjectives.text: Define the top severity tier precisely as complete task failure for an entire AT category, not general severity
Distinguish a genuine blocker from a finding that's merely severe but still completable

contentSections.title: 'Really bad' and 'blocker' are not the same category

contentSections.body: A draft report has eleven findings marked 'Critical.' Reading through them: a data table missing header associations (genuinely confusing, but a patient screen reader user can still work through it cell by cell). A modal with no visible close button, but Escape does close it. A date picker that's awkward but technically operable with a keyboard. And, buried in the same list: a checkout 'Place order' button that's entirely unreachable by keyboard — no tab stop reaches it at all, under any sequence. Eleven items in one bucket, only one of which actually blocks task completion outright.

contentSections.scenario: A severity scale defines its top tier as 'Critical/Blocker: complete failure to complete the task for an entire category of user, with no way around it at all.'
contentSections.question: Applying that precise definition, which of the four findings in the hook actually belongs at that tier?

options.label: All four — they're all serious accessibility problems
Only the unreachable 'Place order' button — the other three are real, serious findings, but each one remains completable, just harder
None of them — 'Critical' should be reserved for legal compliance risk specifically

feedback.all: This is exactly the drift the hook describes — 'serious' and 'blocker' get treated as synonyms, and once that happens the top tier stops meaning anything specific, since eleven different things end up crammed into it at wildly different actual severities.
feedback.one: Right. The confusing data table, the modal, and the awkward date picker are each real, worth-fixing findings — but a determined user can still get through all three and finish the task. The unreachable checkout button cannot be completed by any keyboard-only or screen-reader user, under any sequence, at all. That specific, total failure is what the top tier exists to mean.
feedback.none: Legal risk is a separate axis from task-completion severity, and conflating them narrows 'Critical' to the wrong thing entirely — a genuine complete-blocker finding is Critical regardless of its specific legal exposure.

contentSections.concept: **A blocker means the task cannot be completed at all by an entire category of user — not 'this is really bad,' but 'this is impossible.'** Once 'Critical' starts meaning 'seriously annoying,' it stops meaning anything specific, and a report with eleven Critical findings trains its reader to stop trusting the label — which is the exact opposite of what a severity system is for.

contentSections.body: This precision matters practically, not just semantically: a report where 'Critical' reliably means 'genuinely cannot be done' gives a product team an unambiguous, non-negotiable priority list — these ship-blocking items get fixed before anything else, full stop. A report where 'Critical' has drifted to mean 'quite bad' forces the team to re-triage the entire Critical bucket themselves before they can even start, which is exactly the work the severity rating was supposed to do for them.
Reserve the top severity tier for genuine, complete task failure — a determined user finishing the task the hard way is a serious finding at a lower tier, not a blocker.

contentSections.title: 'For an entire category of user' is doing real work in that definition

contentSections.body: A carousel autoplays and can't be paused. It's genuinely disorienting for someone with a vestibular condition or attention difficulty, and it's a real, citable finding — but it doesn't block anyone from completing the actual task the page exists for (reading the article below it, say). A different finding: a required field's validation error is only ever shown via a colour change, with no text and no icon — meaning a screen reader user gets literally no indication the submission failed at all, and nobody using a screen reader can find out why the form won't submit.

contentSections.question: Why is the second finding a blocker for screen reader users specifically, while the first — genuinely disruptive as it is — isn't a blocker at all?
contentSections.answer: Because 'blocker' is scoped to a specific category of user for whom the task becomes literally impossible, not just unpleasant. A colour-only error with no text or icon means every screen reader user hits a wall with no information to act on — the task genuinely cannot be completed by that entire category, no matter how determined they are. The disorienting carousel is a real, serious problem for some users, but it doesn't stop anyone from completing the underlying task of reading the article — annoying and even harmful is not automatically the same as impossible.
contentSections.hint: Ask, separately for each finding: is there any category of user for whom the actual task simply cannot be finished, versus a category for whom it's unpleasant but still completable?

contentSections.body: Naming the specific affected category explicitly in the finding is what makes a blocker rating defensible rather than assumed: 'blocks all screen reader users from determining why their submission failed' is a precise, checkable claim. 'Blocks users with disabilities' is vague enough to invite exactly the pushback the next lesson's practice set covers — a specific, named category is much harder to argue with than a general one, because it points at exactly who was tested and what happened to them.
A blocker is scoped to a specific, named category of user for whom the task becomes literally impossible — not a general statement that something is bad for accessibility.

title: Conformance level is not severity
description: WCAG's Level A/AA/AAA is a statement about how universally a success criterion applies and how testable it is — not a ranking of how much real-world harm violating it causes. Treating the two as the same axis produces severity ratings that don't track actual impact.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish WCAG conformance level from real-world severity as two genuinely independent properties of a finding
Rate a finding's severity from its actual impact rather than defaulting to its criterion's conformance level

contentSections.title: An AAA finding that's more severe than most A findings

contentSections.body: A junior auditor drafts severity ratings by a simple rule: Level A violations get High severity, Level AA get Medium, Level AAA get Low, because A is 'more required.' Under that rule, a Level AAA sign-language-interpretation gap for a pre-recorded video gets rated Low — while a Level A alt-text issue on a genuinely decorative, meaningless icon gets rated High. For at least one real product this rule was applied to, the video in question was the entire onboarding tutorial, and deaf users without captions or an interpretation track couldn't complete onboarding at all.

contentSections.scenario: The auditor's rule conflates two properties that WCAG's own documentation treats as genuinely separate: conformance level (how universally applicable and objectively testable a criterion is, which determines whether it's required at A, AA, or AAA) and severity (how much real-world harm a specific violation, in this specific context, actually causes).
contentSections.question: What's the mechanism that makes this rule produce wrong severity ratings?

options.label: Nothing — Level A criteria are, by definition, always the most severe kind of accessibility problem
Conformance level measures how universally testable/applicable a criterion is, which is a completely different question from how much harm one specific violation of it causes in one specific context
The rule is fine, but should be reversed — AAA should map to High, since it's the hardest standard to meet

feedback.always-severe: This is precisely the false assumption the hook demonstrates — a genuinely decorative icon's redundant alt text is a real Level A issue that causes essentially no harm, while the onboarding video example shows a Level AAA gap causing complete task failure for an entire group.
feedback.different-axis: Right. WCAG's A/AA/AAA levels are set by how broadly a criterion applies and how objectively it can be tested across all content — not by how much damage any one specific violation causes. A criterion can sit at any conformance level and still, in a specific real context, cause anything from trivial annoyance to complete task failure.
feedback.reversed: Reversing the mapping just moves the same error to the opposite end — it's still treating conformance level as if it predicted severity, when the two are independent by design.

contentSections.mechanism: **Conformance level answers 'how broadly required is this criterion.' Severity answers 'how much does this specific violation actually hurt someone, here, now.'** They're set by entirely different considerations and can land anywhere relative to each other — a Level AAA gap in a mission-critical onboarding video is a real, severe, task-blocking finding regardless of AAA's status as the 'optional, nice-to-have' tier in general.

contentSections.body: This doesn't mean conformance level is useless information — it's the right axis for answering 'what's our minimum legal/contractual obligation here' (most legal frameworks reference AA as the target), and it belongs in the report alongside severity, cited accurately. The mistake is only in treating it as a shortcut for severity, which lets an auditor skip the actual judgement call severity requires — impact, frequency, workaround, per the module's first lesson — in favour of a lookup table that doesn't measure the thing being asked for.

Conformance level measures how universally required a criterion is. Severity measures how much a specific violation actually hurts someone in this specific context. They're independent — cite both, but rate severity on its own merits.

contentSections.title: The finding that's technically Level A and genuinely trivial

contentSections.body: A page's `<html>` element is missing its `lang` attribute — a genuine Level A failure (3.1.1 Language of Page). On this particular site: entirely English content, targeted entirely at an English-speaking audience, with no translation feature and no evidence any user has ever had their screen reader's language auto-switch behaviour affected by it in practice.

contentSections.code: Draft severity note: 'Missing lang attribute — WCAG 3.1.1, Level A. Rated High severity, since Level A criteria represent the minimum legally required baseline and any Level A failure is automatically a compliance risk.'
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this severity reasoning?

options.label: Nothing — Level A failures should always default to High severity for legal safety
The rating is derived entirely from the conformance level, with no actual assessment of real-world impact for this specific site and context
3.1.1 isn't actually a real WCAG success criterion

feedback.nothing: This is exactly the conformance-level-as-severity-shortcut this lesson exists to catch — it produces a rating without ever actually asking what real-world harm this specific instance causes.
feedback.no-impact-assessment: Right. Nothing in the note discusses actual impact — what does a missing lang attribute actually do to a user of this specific, single-language site? In practice, for an entirely English site with no translation or multi-language content, the real-world effect is close to none: screen readers default to the system or browser language regardless, and there's no language-switching behaviour to break.
feedback.not-real: 3.1.1 Language of Page is a real, Level A WCAG success criterion — the issue isn't whether it's real, it's whether this specific instance of violating it causes real harm.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A more defensible note separates the two things explicitly: 'Missing lang attribute — WCAG 3.1.1, Level A (legally relevant as a baseline compliance gap). Severity: Low — this site is single-language English content with no translation feature; the practical effect on screen reader pronunciation and language-switching behaviour is minimal in this specific context. Recommend fixing as a quick, low-cost correction, but it is not a priority ahead of the higher-severity findings in this report.' This keeps the legal/compliance citation accurate while rating severity on what actually happens to a real user of this real site — which, here, is genuinely close to nothing.

contentSections.body: A Level A citation establishes a compliance fact. It doesn't establish severity — that still requires actually asking what this specific violation does to a real user in this specific context.

title: One root cause behind forty findings
description: Forty individual line items can be one shared component's bug, reused forty times — reporting it at the pattern level, with an instance count, is both more accurate and far more actionable than forty separate findings that obscure the one fix that resolves them all.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when a large number of findings share a single root cause worth reporting as one pattern
Write a root-cause finding that states both the shared cause and the full instance count

contentSections.title: Forty line items, one component

contentSections.body: A draft report lists 40 separate findings, each reading something like 'Dropdown on page X has no accessible name' with a different page name each time. Every single one is the exact same custom-built dropdown component, copy-pasted or reused across 40 different pages, with the exact same missing `aria-label`. Forty findings, one bug, one fix.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways to report this. Option A: 40 separate findings, one per page, each with its own severity rating, its own repro steps, its own recommendation. Option B: one finding describing the shared component defect, naming all 40 instances, with one recommendation targeting the shared component definition.
contentSections.question: Which is actually more useful to the team that has to fix this?

options.label: Option A — more line items means the report demonstrates more thoroughness
Option B — one finding naming the shared cause and all instances is both more accurate about what's actually wrong and far more actionable
It doesn't matter, since the total number of affected pages is the same either way

feedback.a: Forty line items for one bug doesn't demonstrate more thoroughness — it obscures the one thing that would actually be useful to know, which is that fixing one shared component fixes all 40 instances at once. A dev team reading 40 separate tickets is more likely to fix a handful and miss the pattern than to realise it's one component-level change.
feedback.b: Right. Naming the shared root cause tells the team exactly where the fix actually needs to happen — the component definition, not 40 individual pages — while still preserving the full instance count so nobody underestimates the defect's real reach or misses that a fix needs verifying across all 40 places it's used.
feedback.same: The total affected surface is the same, but how well the report communicates the actual fix is not — 40 scattered findings actively obscures that this is one bug, not forty, which changes how a team would even approach fixing it.

contentSections.concept: **A root-cause finding names the shared defect once, states every instance it appears in, and points the fix at the actual source.** This isn't about hiding the scale of the problem — the instance count still needs to be full and honest — it's about not obscuring the one fact that would actually change how a team approaches fixing it: this is one bug in one place, not forty independent bugs in forty places.

contentSections.body: Grouping by root cause requires actually verifying the instances share a real cause, not just a surface resemblance — two dropdowns that look similar but were built by different teams with genuinely different underlying code aren't the same finding just because they produce the same symptom. Confirming shared cause (same component, same shared code, same design-system pattern) before grouping is what keeps a root-cause finding accurate rather than a convenient guess.

Forty findings that trace to one shared component are one finding with forty instances — naming the shared cause, and stating the fix at the component level, is more accurate and more actionable than forty separate line items.

contentSections.title: Writing the root-cause finding so nothing gets lost

contentSections.body: A root-cause finding gets written up as 'The dropdown component is missing an accessible name. Recommend fixing the component.' Two weeks later, the fix ships — to the component library's newest version. Fourteen of the forty pages are still on an older, forked version of the component and never got the fix, because nobody actually confirmed which of the forty instances used which version.

contentSections.question: What did the root-cause finding leave out that would have prevented fourteen pages from being missed?
contentSections.answer: The full, explicit instance list — or at minimum, verification of which version of the component each of the 40 instances actually used. 'Fix the component' assumes all 40 instances pull from the same single source, which turned out to be false; without the actual instance-by-instance list, nobody could verify after the fix shipped whether it had actually reached all 40, or catch that 14 of them were on a forked, unpatched version.
contentSections.hint: Think about what 'the fix shipped' actually verified, versus what it should have verified — one central definition changing, or every single instance actually being confirmed fixed.

contentSections.body: A complete root-cause finding states three things together: the shared cause (what's actually wrong, and why it's the same defect everywhere), the full list of affected instances (every page, screen, or component instance — not a representative sample), and the fix location (where the actual change needs to happen). After a fix ships, retesting (covered in this phase's final module) should check the full instance list explicitly, not just the one or two pages someone happened to spot-check — exactly the gap that let fourteen forked instances slip through unnoticed here.

A root-cause finding needs the full instance list stated explicitly, not assumed — 'fix the component' only works if every instance actually shares the same underlying source, and that has to be verified, not guessed.

title: Defending a rating a product owner disputes
description: A product owner arguing a rating is too high isn't automatically wrong, and isn't automatically right — defending a rating means going back to evidence and the impact/frequency/workaround framework, and genuinely updating the rating when new information warrants it.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a legitimate challenge to a severity rating from pressure to lower it without new evidence
Defend or revise a disputed severity rating using the same explicit framework it was originally rated with

contentSections.title: 'That's not really Critical, is it?'

contentSections.body: A finding rated Blocker — a checkout 'Place order' button unreachable by keyboard — gets pushback in a review call: 'Come on, that's not really Critical. Almost nobody uses keyboard-only navigation for checkout specifically.' The auditor has thirty seconds to respond before the conversation moves on.

contentSections.title: Defending the checkout blocker rating
contentSections.opening: The product owner has just pushed back on the Blocker rating for the unreachable 'Place order' button, framing it as an edge case not worth the top severity tier.

respond.situation: You have to respond in the moment, in the same call.
respond.question: What's the strongest first response?

choices.label: Agree to lower it to reduce friction in the meeting, and revisit later if needed
choices.consequence: Conceding without new evidence trains every future dispute to work the same way — pushback, not evidence, becomes what moves a rating.

choices.label: Restate the rating using the same framework it was rated with: impact, frequency, workaround, applied to this specific finding
choices.consequence: This keeps the conversation on the actual evidence rather than on how the finding feels in the room.

choices.label: Push back that the product owner doesn't understand accessibility severity ratings
choices.consequence: This makes the conversation about competence and credibility instead of the actual finding, which tends to escalate rather than resolve.

concede_result.situation: The rating gets lowered in the meeting, on the strength of pushback alone, with no new information about the finding actually presented.
concede_result.question: What's the actual cost of this outcome?

choices.label: Accept it — a slightly lower rating on one finding isn't a big deal in isolation
choices.consequence: In isolation, maybe not — but it establishes that ratings move based on how uncomfortable the room is, not on evidence, which erodes every future rating in the same report.

reassert_result.situation: You say: 'This one's rated Blocker specifically because keyboard-only checkout can't be completed at all — not that it's inconvenient, that it's impossible. That covers keyboard-only users generally, not just people who identify as keyboard-only by preference — anyone with a temporary or situational reason to be without a working mouse or touchscreen hits the identical wall. Is there something about the actual finding I'm missing, or is the concern about how common keyboard-only checkout is?'
reassert_result.question: The product owner replies: 'Fair, I didn't realize it was a hard block, not just harder. I was picturing someone slowly tabbing through — I didn't realize the button literally can't be reached at all.' What's the right next move?

choices.label: Confirm the rating stands, and offer to walk through the repro steps live if useful
choices.consequence: The rating survives on the strength of a precise, evidence-based explanation — exactly what a defensible rating should do.

defensive_result.situation: The conversation shifts to whether the auditor is being condescending, and the actual finding gets lost entirely.
defensive_result.question: What's the cost here?

choices.label: Accept the derailment as an unfortunate but unavoidable cost of the pushback
choices.consequence: It wasn't unavoidable — a framework-based response would have kept the conversation on the finding itself instead of on personalities.

conceded.summary: The rating moved because the room was uncomfortable, not because new evidence emerged.
conceded.lesson: A rating that moves under pressure alone, with no new evidence, teaches everyone in the room that pushback works better than evidence — which is a lesson that costs every other rating in the report, not just this one.

held.summary: Restating the specific impact/frequency/workaround reasoning resolved a genuine misunderstanding without conceding anything the evidence didn't support.
held.lesson: Most disputes aren't actually disagreements about severity — they're a misunderstanding of what was actually found. Restating the precise mechanism, calmly and specifically, resolves far more of these than either conceding or getting defensive.

derailed.summary: The conversation became about credibility instead of the finding, and nothing about the actual rating got resolved.
derailed.lesson: Defensiveness invites the room to relitigate the auditor's competence instead of the evidence — a framework-based, calm restatement keeps the finding itself at the centre of the conversation.

contentSections.body: Most disputes are a misunderstanding of what was actually found, not a genuine disagreement about severity — restating the specific impact/frequency/workaround reasoning resolves far more of them than conceding or getting defensive.

contentSections.title: When the pushback is actually right

contentSections.body: In a different review, a product owner disputes a High-severity rating on a finding by pointing out something the auditor genuinely didn't know: the affected page is a legacy admin tool being fully decommissioned in three weeks, used by exactly two internal staff members who have already been individually notified and have an alternative process in place. This is a genuinely different situation from the checkout example, and deserves a genuinely different response — here, real new information has actually been introduced.

contentSections.scenario: The auditor lowers the finding's severity after hearing the decommissioning and staff-notification information, and documents the specific reason for the change in the report.
contentSections.question: What makes this a legitimate revision rather than the same 'caved to pressure' failure from the checkout example?

options.label: It isn't legitimate — a rating should never change once published, regardless of new information

It's legitimate because genuinely new information changed a real input to the framework (frequency, workaround) — the rating is being re-derived from the same method with better facts, not abandoned under discomfort
It's only legitimate because a product owner, specifically, asked for it — pushback from anyone senior enough should always move a rating

feedback.never-change: A rating that can never update even in light of genuinely new, verified facts isn't rigor — it's just as arbitrary as a rating that moves for no reason at all, in the opposite direction.
feedback.legitimate: Right. The distinction isn't 'did the rating change' — it's whether the change came from new facts that genuinely feed the same framework, or from discomfort alone with no new information. Here, real facts changed two of the three explicit inputs (frequency and workaround), so re-deriving the rating from those updated facts is the framework working correctly, not being abandoned.
feedback.seniority: Whose title is attached to the pushback has nothing to do with whether the underlying facts actually changed — the same update would be equally legitimate coming from anyone with the same new information, and equally illegitimate from a product owner offering no new facts at all.

contentSections.mechanism: **The test for a legitimate revision is whether a real input to the framework actually changed, not whether someone senior was uncomfortable.** Impact, frequency, and workaround are the three explicit things that determine a rating — if genuinely new, verifiable information changes one of them, updating the rating is the framework doing its job. If nothing about the finding's actual facts has changed and the rating moves anyway, that's the framework being overridden by pressure, which is a different thing entirely.

contentSections.body: A rating built honestly from impact, frequency and workaround should update when one of those three inputs actually changes — refusing to update it at that point would be defending the original number for its own sake, rather than defending what the framework actually says given the new facts. That's the difference worth holding onto: the framework isn't a fixed answer to be defended forever, it's a method that gets re-run honestly whenever the real facts feeding it change.

A rating should update when a real input — impact, frequency, or workaround — genuinely changes based on new, verified information. It shouldn't update because a room got uncomfortable with no new facts at all.

title: Practice — Rate and Defend Severity for Eight Findings
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where rating severity precisely, and holding a rating under real pushback, stops being something you've read about and becomes something you can do fast and defend.

learningObjectives.text: Apply impact/frequency/workaround rating and root-cause grouping to unfamiliar findings at speed
Distinguish a legitimate reason to revise a severity rating from pressure to lower it with no new evidence

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or spread across a few — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Prioritise a Hundred-Finding Backlog
description: Take a large, messy list of findings and turn it into a real prioritised backlog: rated by impact/frequency/workaround, grouped by root cause where it's genuinely justified, with a stated rationale for every rating.

learningObjectives.text: Rate a large set of findings for severity using impact, frequency and workaround consistently
Group findings by genuinely verified root cause without over- or under-grouping
Produce a prioritised backlog with a stated rationale a stakeholder could defend or dispute on its merits

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This lab works from a provided or self-assembled list of findings (real findings from your own testing across this phase's prior labs work well, or a fresh set from a product you test now) — the point is turning an unordered pile into a defensible, prioritised backlog.

contentSections.title: Prioritise a hundred-finding backlog
contentSections.brief: Assemble or reuse a substantial list of findings (aim for at least 15-20 for this exercise to be meaningful, standing in for a full hundred-finding audit). Rate each for severity using impact, frequency and workaround explicitly. Identify and group any findings that share a genuinely verified root cause. Produce a final prioritised backlog with a stated rationale for every rating.
contentSections.deliverable: A prioritised backlog grouped by root cause where justified, with a stated rating rationale for every item.

stages.title: Assemble and rate each finding
stages.instructions: For each finding, rate severity explicitly using impact (does it block the task?), frequency (how often would a real user hit it?), and workaround (is there a genuine, non-destructive way around it?). Write a one-line rationale for each rating using these three terms explicitly.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has an explicit severity rating and a rationale naming impact, frequency and workaround specifically — not a gut-feeling number.

stages.title: Identify and group root causes
stages.instructions: Look for findings that might share a root cause. For each candidate group, verify the shared cause is real (same component, same shared code) before grouping — don't group on symptom resemblance alone. Write each verified group as one finding with a full instance list and a fix location.
stages.checkpoint: Any grouped findings have a verified, stated shared cause, a complete instance list, and a specific fix location — nothing is grouped on appearance alone.

stages.title: Produce the final prioritised backlog and self-check
stages.instructions: Order the final list by severity, with root-cause groups appearing as single entries. Read through once as if a stakeholder were about to dispute the top three ratings — check that each has a defensible, specific rationale ready. Then run the self-check below.
stages.checkpoint: Every rubric criterion below is met, or you've noted specifically what's still missing.

rubric.criterion: Every rating is derived from impact, frequency and workaround explicitly
rubric.meets: A reader can see the specific reasoning behind every severity rating, not just a number.

rubric.criterion: Blocker-tier ratings meet the strict definition
rubric.meets: Every finding rated at the top tier represents genuine, complete task failure for a named category of user — not just a severe-sounding finding.

rubric.criterion: Conformance level and severity are kept independent
rubric.meets: No rating is derived by defaulting to the finding's WCAG conformance level rather than assessing its actual impact.

rubric.criterion: Root-cause groups are verified, not assumed
rubric.meets: Any grouped finding names the actual shared cause, the complete instance list, and the fix location — nothing is grouped on symptom resemblance alone.

rubric.criterion: Every top-priority rating is defensible under real pushback
rubric.meets: For the highest-rated findings, you could restate the specific impact/frequency/workaround reasoning on the spot if challenged.

contentSections.body: A backlog you've never actually prioritised from a messy list is a framework you've only read about — this lab is the difference between knowing the three questions and having applied them consistently across a real, sizeable set of findings.

title: Checkpoint — Severity and Prioritisation
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the module before it, and further back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core severity distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Severity and Prioritisation

questions.prompt: What are the three explicit inputs to a severity rating covered in this module?

options.label: Impact, frequency, and whether there's a genuine workaround
WCAG conformance level, criterion number, and the fix's estimated cost
How many testers found it, how long it took to find, and its position in the report

questions.explanation: Severity is rated from impact (does it block the task), frequency (how often a real user hits it), and workaround (is there a genuine, reliable way around it) — three separate, explicit questions.

questions.prompt: A user could technically avoid a barrier by guessing which of two unlabelled buttons is 'Submit' versus 'Clear all data.' Does this count as a real workaround?

options.label: No — a real workaround has to be reliable and knowable in advance; guessing wrong here has a real, destructive cost
Yes — any way to eventually complete the task counts as a workaround
Yes, but only if the user guesses correctly on the first try

questions.explanation: A genuine workaround needs to be reliable and knowable in advance, not discovered through a costly guess — trial and error next to a destructive action isn't a real workaround.

questions.prompt: What does the top severity tier ('Blocker'/'Critical') precisely mean in this module's framework?

options.label: Complete task failure for an entire named category of user, with no way around it — not just 'seriously bad'
Any finding that violates a Level A success criterion
Any finding a stakeholder personally finds especially embarrassing

questions.explanation: A blocker means the task genuinely cannot be completed at all by an entire category of user — a determined user who can still finish the task the hard way belongs at a lower tier.

questions.prompt: Why is 'this violates a Level A criterion, so it's automatically High severity' a flawed approach?

options.label: Conformance level measures how universally required a criterion is, not how much real-world harm a specific violation causes — the two are independent
Level A criteria are actually less severe than Level AAA on average
It isn't flawed — this is the correct, standard way to derive severity

questions.explanation: A Level AAA gap can cause complete task failure in the right context, and a Level A finding can be nearly harmless in the right context — conformance level and severity are genuinely independent properties.

questions.prompt: 40 findings all trace to the same shared dropdown component's missing accessible name. What's the better way to report this?

options.label: One finding naming the shared cause, listing all 40 instances explicitly, and pointing the fix at the component definition
40 separate findings, since more line items demonstrate more thoroughness
One finding with no instance list, just stating 'this appears in many places'

questions.explanation: A root-cause finding should name the shared cause, list every instance explicitly (not just note that there are many), and point the fix at the actual source — this is both more accurate and more actionable than 40 scattered line items.

questions.prompt: After a root-cause fix ships to a shared component, what should happen next?

options.label: Verify the fix against the full original instance list explicitly — a component-level change doesn't guarantee it reached every listed instance (some may be on a forked or unpatched version)
Assume all instances are fixed automatically, since the shared component was updated
Spot-check only the single highest-severity instance

questions.explanation: A component-level fix can miss instances on a forked or divergent version — the full original instance list needs explicit re-verification, not an assumption that the shared update reached everywhere.

questions.prompt: A product owner disputes a rating with 'I just don't think this is as bad as you're saying,' offering no new fact. What's the right response?

options.label: Calmly restate the specific impact/frequency/workaround reasoning behind the original rating
Lower the rating to reduce friction in the conversation
Argue that the product owner doesn't understand accessibility

questions.explanation: With no new fact introduced, restating the specific framework-based reasoning is what resolves most disputes — they're usually a misunderstanding of what was actually found, not a genuine disagreement.

questions.prompt: When is it legitimate to revise a severity rating after pushback?

options.label: When genuinely new, verifiable information changes a real input to the framework — impact, frequency, or workaround — not merely because someone is uncomfortable with the number
Never — a published rating should never change under any circumstances
Whenever the pushback comes from someone senior enough

questions.explanation: The test is whether a real input to the framework actually changed based on new facts, not whether the room was uncomfortable or who raised the objection.

questions.from: Previous module — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: A finding a developer can't reproduce because the repro steps are vague is functionally what?

options.label: Not yet a real finding — more of a lead, since nothing in it can be acted on without guesswork
Still a complete finding, just poorly formatted
Only a problem if the developer is inexperienced

questions.explanation: A finding a developer can't reproduce is functionally not a finding yet — exact steps, environment, and expected-versus-actual behaviour are what turn a lead into something actionable.

questions.prompt: Why is a journey-based sample more likely to catch a task-blocking barrier than a page-by-page sample?

options.label: Most task-blocking barriers live in transitional states — a modal, a validation error, a step change — that a page inventory never visits because they don't have their own URL
Journeys always cover more total pages than a page-by-page sample
Page-by-page samples are only useful for very small sites

questions.explanation: A page inventory tests whether templates conform in isolation; a journey forces a tester through the transitional states — modals, errors, step changes — where task-blocking barriers actually tend to live.

contentSections.body: None of these need to be perfect. What matters is which ones needed a guess — that's what the next checkpoint will bring back.

title: The report structure that gets read
description: A 90-page report in one long narrative gets skimmed once and never opened again. A structure that front-loads what matters to each specific reader — executive, developer, project manager — is what actually gets used after delivery day.

learningObjectives.text: Design a report structure that serves an executive reader and a developer reader without making either dig for what they need
Explain why front-loading the most consequential information changes whether a report gets used after delivery

contentSections.title: The 90-page report nobody opens twice

contentSections.body: A completed audit is delivered as a single 90-page PDF: a long narrative introduction, then findings in the order they happened to be discovered during testing, with severity and WCAG citations buried mid-paragraph inside each one. It gets opened once, skimmed for ten minutes, and — six weeks later, when a developer needs to know exactly what's wrong with the checkout flow specifically — nobody can find that section again without searching the whole document.

contentSections.scenario: Two structures for the same audit. Structure A: one continuous narrative, findings ordered by when they were discovered during testing, severity mentioned in passing within each paragraph. Structure B: executive summary first, then methodology and scope, then findings grouped by severity (highest first) with a consistent, scannable format for each, then an appendix with full technical detail.
contentSections.question: Which structure is more likely to actually get used weeks after delivery, not just skimmed once?

options.label: Structure A — a narrative reads more naturally and tells the story of the audit
Structure B — front-loading what matters most, and making every finding scannable in a consistent format, means someone can find what they need without rereading the whole thing
It doesn't matter — the same information is present in both

feedback.a: A narrative reads well the first time through, but nobody re-reads a 90-page narrative to find one specific piece of information six weeks later — they need to be able to jump directly to it, which order-of-discovery doesn't support.
feedback.b: Right. The same information present in a different order and format changes whether a report actually gets used as a working document versus read once and shelved. Severity-first ordering with a consistent per-finding format means a developer can jump straight to what matters, and an executive never has to read past page one to get the headline.
feedback.same: Having the same information present isn't the same as having it usable — findability and scannability are themselves part of what makes a report actually useful after delivery day, not incidental formatting choices.

contentSections.concept: **A report structure should be built around how it will actually be used afterward, not the order the testing happened to occur in.** An executive reads the first page and needs the headline. A developer needs to jump straight to their specific finding, months later, without re-reading everything around it. A structure ordered by discovery serves neither — it only reflects the auditor's own process, not either reader's actual need.

contentSections.body: A structure that serves both readers, front to back: an executive summary (covered in depth in this module's fourth lesson) stating the overall picture in a page or less; methodology and scope (what was tested, how, and what wasn't — pulling directly from the scope document this phase's first module produced); findings grouped by severity, highest first, each in a consistent, scannable format; and a technical appendix for anything too detailed to belong in the main findings list (full environment logs, raw automated scan output). Nothing here is new information — it's the same content, organised around who needs which part and when.

This connects directly back to the scoping work done at the start of the phase: the methodology section isn't written from scratch at report time, it's essentially the scope document's sample, matrix, and exclusions restated as what was actually done — which is also exactly why keeping that scope document accurate and updated (per the earlier lesson on revisiting scope when the facts change) pays off directly here, rather than requiring the auditor to reconstruct what was tested from memory weeks later.

Structure the report around how each reader will actually use it — an executive needs the headline on page one, a developer needs to jump straight to their finding months later — not around the order testing happened to occur in.

contentSections.title: A consistent format is what makes a finding scannable

contentSections.body: One finding in a draft report is three paragraphs of flowing prose. The next is a bulleted list. The one after that opens with the WCAG citation, the one after that buries the citation in the third sentence. A developer trying to quickly scan fifteen findings for the ones relevant to their part of the codebase has to fully read each one, since nothing about the format tells them where to look first.

contentSections.question: What does a consistent, repeated format across every single finding actually buy a reader, compared to well-written prose that varies finding to finding?
contentSections.answer: Scannability. Once a reader learns where severity, location, and recommendation live in the first finding's format, they can scan every subsequent finding for just the parts they need — jump straight to severity to triage, or straight to location to check if it's their part of the codebase — without reading the whole thing every time. Varied prose, even if each individual finding reads beautifully on its own, forces a full read every time because nothing about the format is predictable from one finding to the next.
contentSections.hint: Think about what changes for a reader on finding number twelve, once they've already read findings one through eleven in the same format versus in eleven different formats.

contentSections.body: A workable consistent format, in a fixed order every time: a short, specific title naming the actual problem (not 'Accessibility issue #14'); severity; WCAG citation (where genuinely applicable, per the earlier module's honesty about findings with no clean citation); location (exact page/component); a one-line user-impact statement (this phase's second module's evidence work feeds directly into this); and a recommendation. The next lesson goes into what belongs in each of these fields specifically — the point here is that the same fields, in the same order, every single time, is what turns fifteen findings into something a reader can actually navigate.

The same fields, in the same order, for every single finding, is what turns a report into something a reader can scan and navigate — not a collection of well-written individual paragraphs that each have to be read in full.

title: A finding: what, where, who it affects, what to do
description: Every finding needs the same four things stated explicitly, no matter how obvious any one of them seems in context: exactly what's wrong, exactly where, exactly who it affects and how, and exactly what to do about it.

learningObjectives.text: Write a finding that states what, where, who, and what-to-do explicitly rather than leaving any one implicit
Identify which of the four elements is missing from an incomplete finding

contentSections.title: The finding missing the one thing that actually mattered

contentSections.body: A finding reads: 'The date picker component has accessibility issues. WCAG 2.1.1, 4.1.2. High severity. Recommend fixing.' Every field technically has something in it. A developer reading it still has no idea what's actually wrong, where the component is used, who's affected, or what 'fixing' means concretely.

contentSections.scenario: Checking this finding against the four things every finding needs: what's wrong, where, who's affected, what to do.
contentSections.question: Which of these four does the finding above actually deliver in a usable form? Select all that genuinely apply.

items.label: What's wrong — a specific, concrete description of the actual defect
Where — the exact location (page, component, instance)
Who's affected and how — the specific user impact
What to do — a specific, actionable recommendation

explanation.what: No — 'has accessibility issues' names nothing specific. Two citation numbers are listed, but neither is tied to an actual described defect.
explanation.where: No — 'the date picker component' doesn't say which page it's on, or whether it's one instance or many (echoing the root-cause instance-list discipline from the previous module).
explanation.who: No — nothing states what actually happens to a real user, or which category of user is affected.
explanation.citation: Yes — this is the one thing genuinely present, though without a described defect attached to it, even the citation is hard to verify or act on.
explanation.what-to-do: No — 'recommend fixing' gives no indication of what a fix would actually involve.

contentSections.synthesis: A finding can have a citation, a severity label, and a title, and still be functionally useless if it never states the specific defect, its exact location, its real user impact, or a concrete recommendation. Each of the four needs its own explicit sentence — none of them can be safely assumed to be 'obvious enough' from the others.

contentSections.body: A usable version of the same finding: 'What: the date field in the booking form doesn't announce the selected date to screen reader users after selection — visually the field updates, but nothing is communicated via the accessibility tree. Where: the shared DatePicker component, confirmed present on the booking form, the profile birth-date field, and the event-creation form (3 instances). Who: any screen reader user selecting a date anywhere this component is used cannot confirm what date is currently selected without switching to visual inspection. What to do: the selected date needs to be exposed to assistive technology when it changes — for example, via an aria-live region announcing the new value, or by ensuring the underlying input's value update is itself exposed to the accessibility tree.'
Every finding needs what, where, who, and what-to-do stated as its own explicit sentence — a citation and a severity label alone don't substitute for any of the four.

contentSections.title: Making 'who it affects' concrete instead of generic

contentSections.body: A finding's user-impact line reads: 'This affects users with disabilities.' Every finding in a 60-finding report has an identical version of this same sentence, which communicates essentially nothing about any individual finding beyond the fact that it exists in an accessibility report at all.

contentSections.scenario: The impact statement is technically true for every finding in the report, which is exactly why it fails to communicate anything useful about any specific one.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that makes a generic impact statement like this fail?

options.label: It's factually inaccurate
It's true of every finding equally, which means it conveys zero information distinguishing one finding's real impact from another's
It should be replaced with a specific disability diagnosis instead

feedback.inaccurate: The statement isn't false — the issue is that being true of literally everything in the report makes it useless as a distinguishing description of any one finding.
feedback.no-info: Right. A statement that would be equally true if pasted onto any other finding in the report carries no information about this specific finding's actual, particular impact. The whole point of the impact field is to say something specific enough that it couldn't just be copy-pasted onto a different finding unchanged.
feedback.diagnosis: Naming a specific medical diagnosis is neither necessary nor appropriate — the useful specificity is about the functional impact (what task, blocked how, for whom by category of tool or need), not a medical label.

contentSections.mechanism: **A useful impact statement names the specific task, the specific mechanism of the barrier, and the specific category of user by their actual relationship to the interface — not a diagnosis.** 'Screen reader users cannot confirm which date is currently selected' is specific to this finding and this task. 'Users with disabilities' is true of the whole report and specific to nothing — it could be pasted onto any finding in the document without anyone noticing it was moved.

contentSections.body: A useful impact statement names the specific task, the specific mechanism, and the specific category of user affected — a generic 'users with disabilities' sentence that would fit any finding in the report communicates nothing about this one.

title: Recommending a fix without designing it for them
description: A recommendation should describe the outcome a fix needs to achieve, not a specific implementation the auditor hasn't actually verified fits the team's codebase — over-specifying a fix can be as unhelpful as under-specifying one.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish an outcome-focused recommendation from one that over-prescribes an implementation the auditor can't verify fits
Write a recommendation specific enough to act on without dictating exact code the auditor hasn't seen the surrounding context for

contentSections.title: The recommendation that assumes a codebase the auditor has never seen

contentSections.body: A finding recommends: 'Add `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"` to the `<div class="status-message">` element, and wrap the confirmation text in a `<span>` with `role="status"`.' The auditor has never seen this codebase's actual markup — the recommendation happens to be roughly correct for one plausible implementation, but the class name and structure are guesses, and the actual element might be a React component with a completely different internal structure that makes this exact snippet meaningless.

contentSections.code:
Recommendation, as written:
'Add aria-live="polite" and aria-atomic="true" to the <div class="status-message"> element, and wrap the confirmation text in a <span> with role="status".'
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw here, given the auditor doesn't have access to the real codebase?

options.label: Nothing is wrong — specific code is always more helpful than a general description

It prescribes an exact implementation (specific class names, specific element structure) the auditor hasn't actually verified matches the real codebase, which can be actively wrong or confusing if the real structure differs
aria-live and role="status" should never both be recommended together

feedback.nothing: Specific code is more helpful only when it's actually correct for the real codebase — code that happens to be guessed correctly is helpful by luck, and code that's guessed wrong (a different class name, a component library that doesn't work this way) can send a developer down the wrong path entirely.
feedback.over-specified: Right. The auditor is describing an implementation they haven't verified against the actual code — the specific class name is a guess, and the actual markup could be produced by a component library, a templating system, or a structure completely different from what's written here. A developer following this literally, if it doesn't match, either gets confused or has to redo the actual analysis the recommendation implied was already done.
feedback.combo-wrong: This combination is a real, valid pattern in the right context — the problem isn't the technique itself, it's applying it as a literal prescription without knowing whether it fits the actual codebase.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The auditor's actual job is identifying the outcome that needs to be achieved (a status change needs to be announced to assistive technology) and, where useful, naming the class of technique that achieves it (a live region, or ensuring the framework's own state-update mechanism triggers an accessible announcement) — not writing final code for a codebase they haven't inspected. A better version: 'The confirmation message needs to be announced to assistive technology when it appears — this is typically achieved with an ARIA live region (aria-live) on the container that receives the message, or by using your framework's accessible announcement utility if one exists. The specific implementation will depend on how this component currently renders; happy to review the actual markup if useful.'

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument for vagueness — 'make it more accessible' is exactly as unhelpful in the opposite direction, since it gives a developer nothing concrete to act on at all. The right level of specificity names the outcome precisely (what needs to be true when the fix is done) and the general technique or pattern that gets there, while stopping short of dictating exact syntax for code the auditor hasn't actually seen.

A recommendation should name the outcome precisely and the general technique that achieves it — dictating exact code for a codebase the auditor hasn't inspected can be as unhelpful, in a different way, as being too vague to act on at all.

contentSections.title: When exact code genuinely is the right call

contentSections.body: A finding involves a specific, well-known WCAG technique with essentially one standard correct implementation: a visually-hidden-but-focusable skip link. Here, the actual CSS technique (position: absolute, off-screen until focused, then repositioned on :focus) is close to universal and not really codebase-specific in the way a live-region implementation inside a specific component framework is.

contentSections.question: Does the 'describe the outcome, not the exact code' rule mean an auditor should never include a code snippet in a recommendation?
contentSections.answer: No — it means being honest about which category a given fix falls into. A near-universal, framework-agnostic technique (the visually-hidden-but-focusable skip link CSS pattern, for instance) is safe to show as an actual snippet, since it isn't really guessing at the client's specific codebase structure. A fix that depends on how a specific component is built (a live region inside one particular framework's state-management pattern) is where showing invented, unverified code risks being actively wrong — there, describing the outcome and the general technique, and offering to review the real code, is the honest move.
contentSections.hint: Think about the actual difference between the skip-link CSS pattern and the earlier aria-live example — is one of them closer to 'the same everywhere' than the other?

contentSections.body: The judgement call, each time: is this technique close to universal regardless of the underlying codebase (safe to show as real code), or does the correct implementation genuinely depend on how this specific product is built (safer to describe as an outcome and offer to review the real markup)? Getting this distinction right is itself part of what makes a recommendation trustworthy — a developer who gets one over-specific, wrong-for-their-codebase recommendation is likely to distrust every other recommendation in the same report, even the ones that were genuinely correct.

A near-universal technique is safe to show as real code. A fix that depends on the client's specific codebase structure is safer described as an outcome and a general technique, with an offer to review the actual implementation.

title: The executive summary that doesn't lie by omission
description: An executive summary that spins 'mostly compliant' when three blockers exist is dishonest by omission, even if every individual sentence in it is technically true — the discipline is stating the real risk plainly, without either doom or minimisation.

learningObjectives.text: Write an executive summary that states real risk honestly without either overstating or understating it
Identify when a technically-true summary is still misleading by omission

contentSections.title: Technically true, still misleading

contentSections.body: An audit finds 3 Blocker-severity findings (complete task failure for entire categories of users) among 60 total findings. The executive summary reads: 'The vast majority of pages tested — 57 of 60 findings — were rated Medium or below, reflecting a generally solid accessibility foundation with room for improvement.' Every number in that sentence is accurate. It's also the kind of sentence that lets a reader who only reads the summary walk away without ever learning that 3 people-cannot-complete-the-core-task findings exist at all.

contentSections.scenario: Every individual fact in the summary is verifiably true — the counts are correct, 'generally solid' is a defensible characterisation of 57 out of 60 findings taken alone.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that makes this summary dishonest despite being factually accurate?

options.label: It isn't dishonest — every stated fact is true, and a summary can't be blamed for what it doesn't include

It's dishonest by omission — foregrounding a true-but-reassuring statistic while omitting the three most consequential findings entirely lets a reader form a false overall impression from accurate individual facts
It's dishonest because the percentage calculation is wrong

feedback.not-dishonest: A summary absolutely can be blamed for what it omits — the entire function of a summary is choosing what to foreground, and choosing to foreground a reassuring statistic while leaving out the three most severe findings is itself a choice with real consequences for what the reader takes away.
feedback.omission: Right. Individually true facts, selectively arranged, can produce a false overall impression — this is the textbook shape of lying by omission. 'Generally solid, with room for improvement' actively misdescribes a product with three genuine task-blocking failures, even though every underlying number cited is correct.
feedback.math: The math itself isn't the problem — 57/60 is accurate. The problem is which facts got chosen to represent the whole picture, not whether the arithmetic is right.

contentSections.mechanism: **A summary's job is representing the real overall picture, not just stating individually true facts in a flattering arrangement.** The three Blocker findings are, by definition (per the earlier module's precise use of that term), the most consequential facts in the entire audit — a summary that a reader could finish without learning they exist has failed at its actual job, regardless of how accurate every individual sentence in it happens to be.
