contentSections.body: A summary built from individually true facts can still be dishonest by omission if it foregrounds a reassuring statistic while leaving out the most consequential findings entirely — a reader shouldn't be able to finish it without knowing the real headline.

contentSections.title: Honest doesn't mean alarmist either

contentSections.body: A different draft executive summary opens: 'This product is riddled with severe accessibility failures that expose the organisation to significant legal risk and actively harm disabled users at every turn.' The audit actually found 2 genuine Blockers among 45 findings, most of which are real but moderate — the summary is now overstating the picture in the opposite direction. Overcorrecting toward alarmism has a real cost beyond tone: a summary that reads as exaggerated relative to the actual findings list teaches a stakeholder to discount the auditor's severity language generally, burying the two genuine Blockers under language that reads as equally intense for everything — the same practical failure as the earlier module's 'eleven Critical findings' problem, just at the summary level.

contentSections.problem: Write an honest executive summary for an audit that found 2 genuine Blocker findings (checkout unreachable by keyboard; a required CAPTCHA with no alternative) among 45 total findings, most of which are real but moderate-severity.

steps.label: State the headline plainly, without either burying or inflating it
steps.work: 'This audit identified 45 findings, including 2 that block task completion entirely for specific user groups: the checkout flow cannot be completed via keyboard at all, and a required CAPTCHA has no accessible alternative, blocking anyone unable to complete it visually.'
steps.why: This states the two most consequential facts specifically and plainly, in the first substantive sentence — not buried in a statistic, and not inflated with language ('riddled with,' 'actively harm... at every turn') the actual severity distribution doesn't support.

steps.label: Give the overall distribution honestly, without letting it dilute the headline
steps.work: 'The remaining 43 findings range from Moderate to Low severity and represent real, worthwhile improvements rather than task-blocking barriers.'
steps.why: This is honest about the fact that most findings aren't blockers, without implying the 2 that are should be read as a minor footnote to an otherwise-fine picture.

steps.label: State the practical implication clearly
steps.work: 'We recommend addressing the 2 Blocker findings before the next release, given they prevent task completion entirely for the affected users; the remaining findings can be prioritised into the normal development cycle per the severity ratings in the full report.'
steps.why: This gives a stakeholder a clear, actionable read of what the numbers actually mean for what to do next — the whole point of an executive summary.

faded.problem: A different audit: 0 Blocker findings, 3 High-severity findings (each affecting a meaningful but bounded group — one journey each), and 30 lower-severity findings.

blanks.prompt: How should the headline sentence handle the absence of any Blocker findings, honestly?
blanks.answer: State plainly that no task-blocking failures were found, while still naming the 3 High-severity findings specifically rather than letting 'no blockers' read as 'nothing serious' — e.g. 'No findings blocked task completion outright; 3 High-severity findings affect specific journeys and are worth prioritising.'
accept: state no blockers exist, but name the 3 High findings specifically so it doesn't read as "everything is fine"
blanks.why: Omitting the 3 High findings just because nothing hit the very top tier would repeat the same omission problem from this lesson's first pod, one severity level down.

blanks.prompt: How should the overall distribution be framed honestly here?
blanks.answer: Something like '30 additional findings are Moderate or below, representing real opportunities for improvement rather than urgent risks' — accurate to the actual distribution, neither inflated nor dismissive.
accept: an accurate, non-alarmist, non-dismissive description of the remaining 30 findings
blanks.why: The same discipline applies regardless of severity level — describe what's actually there, not a flattering or alarming distortion of it.

blanks.prompt: What's the honest practical recommendation here?
blanks.answer: Prioritise the 3 High-severity findings in the near term (even without a hard blocker deadline pressure), and schedule the remaining 30 into normal development cycles by severity.
accept: recommend addressing the 3 High findings with real priority, and folding the rest into normal prioritisation
blanks.why: The practical recommendation should track the real severity distribution — not treat an absence of Blockers as license to deprioritise the High findings that do exist.

contentSections.procedure: State the most consequential facts plainly and specifically in the opening, give the overall distribution honestly without letting it dilute or inflate the headline, and end with a clear, proportionate practical recommendation — the same discipline whether the real picture is severe, moderate, or genuinely reassuring.

contentSections.body: Honest doesn't mean alarmist any more than it means minimising — state the real headline plainly and specifically, give the real distribution without spin in either direction, and let the actual findings determine the tone, not a house style.

title: Reports that don't shame the team who wrote the code
description: The same finding can be written about a system-level pattern or about a person's failure — one produces a team that fixes things faster, the other produces a team that gets defensive and reads every future finding as an attack.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a finding's language is framed on the system/pattern versus on an individual or team, and rewrite it accordingly
Explain why blame-coded language in a report makes the underlying problems harder, not easier, to get fixed

contentSections.title: The finding that reads like an accusation

contentSections.body: A finding reads: 'The developers failed to add alt text to 40 images across the site, a basic requirement they should have known about. This carelessness affects blind users significantly.' Every fact in it might well be accurate. It's also written in a way that a developer reading it — quite possibly someone who joined the team after those 40 images were added, or who inherited a component from someone who left two years ago — experiences as a personal accusation rather than a description of something to fix.

contentSections.scenario: Two versions of essentially the same finding. Version A: 'The developers failed to add alt text... a basic requirement they should have known about... this carelessness affects blind users significantly.' Version B: '40 images across the site are missing alt text, meaning blind users using a screen reader receive no description of their content or purpose. Recommend adding a content-writing pass for alt text as part of the image-upload workflow, so it becomes a standard step rather than something added after the fact.'
contentSections.question: Which version is more likely to actually get the underlying problem fixed, and fixed durably?

options.label: Version A — naming the failure directly holds the team accountable and motivates faster action
Version B — describing the system-level gap and a process fix addresses the actual cause without triggering defensiveness that slows everything down
Both are equally effective, since the underlying facts and recommendation are the same

feedback.a: Language that reads as a personal accusation ('failed,' 'should have known,' 'carelessness') tends to trigger defensiveness rather than fast action — a team that feels attacked is more likely to argue about the framing than to move quickly on the actual fix, and a defensive team also reads every subsequent finding in the report through the same lens.
feedback.b: Right. Version B describes exactly the same underlying facts and recommends exactly the same real action, but frames it as a system gap (alt text isn't currently part of the upload workflow) with a system-level fix (make it part of the workflow) — which is both more useful (it prevents recurrence, not just fixes the 40 existing instances) and far less likely to produce a defensive reaction that slows the whole engagement down.
feedback.same: The facts and the concrete recommendation are the same, but the framing genuinely changes how the reader receives it — 'failed,' 'should have known,' and 'carelessness' are all judgement of the people, not description of the system, and that difference has a real, measurable effect on how a report actually lands.

contentSections.concept: **Frame every finding on the system or pattern, not on the people who happened to write the code.** 'The upload workflow doesn't currently require alt text' describes a gap in a process. 'The developers failed to' describes a person's inadequacy. The underlying fact and the concrete fix can be identical — the difference in framing is the entire difference between a team that moves fast to fix it and a team that gets defensive first.

contentSections.body: Frame findings on the system or the pattern — a workflow gap, a missing process step — rather than on the people who happened to write the code. Same facts, same fix, dramatically different reception.

contentSections.title: Being honest about severity without being unkind about cause

contentSections.body: This isn't a call to soften severity ratings or hide real problems to spare feelings — the earlier lesson on honest executive summaries and the module's whole discipline of accurate severity still apply in full. A genuine Blocker is still a Blocker, described plainly. The question here is specifically about the language surrounding the description, not about understating what was actually found.

contentSections.code:
Finding, attempting to be both honest and kind:
'Unfortunately, and we mean this gently, the checkout button is completely unreachable by keyboard, which is honestly a pretty basic thing to have missed and reflects poorly on the QA process here. Severity: Low, since we don't want to be too harsh.'
contentSections.question: This finding gets the tone half right and one thing badly wrong. What's the actual flaw?

options.label: Nothing is wrong — softening the severity rating is the correct way to be kind about a difficult finding
It downgrades the severity rating specifically to avoid discomfort, which misrepresents the actual, genuine blocker-level impact — kindness in tone shouldn't mean dishonesty in the rating itself
It's too kind and should be rewritten to be more blunt about the team's failure

feedback.softening-ok: Softening a severity rating to spare feelings is a real problem, not a solution — it misrepresents the actual, verified impact of the finding, which is exactly the dishonesty-by-omission failure from the previous lesson, just motivated by kindness instead of PR concerns.
feedback.downgraded: Right. 'Completely unreachable by keyboard' on a checkout flow meets the precise definition of a Blocker from the earlier module — rating it Low specifically to avoid discomfort is a real, serious accuracy problem, not a kindness. The 'reflects poorly on the QA process' line is also still blame-coded language despite the gentler wrapping.
feedback.too-kind: The problem isn't that it's too kind in tone — a kind, system-focused tone is exactly the goal. The problem is that kindness got applied to the wrong thing: the severity rating, which needs to stay accurate, instead of the framing language, which is where kindness actually belongs.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A version that gets both right: 'The checkout "Place order" button is entirely unreachable by keyboard — no tab sequence reaches it. This is a Blocker: keyboard-only users cannot complete a purchase at all. This is a common gap in custom-built interactive components, especially ones that started as click-only prototypes; recommend adding this specifically to the QA checklist for any new interactive component going forward, alongside a fix for this instance.' The severity stays accurate and unsoftened. The framing stays on the system (a common gap in custom components, a process fix for the future) rather than on the people ('reflects poorly on the QA process'). Kindness belongs in the language around the finding, never in the accuracy of the rating itself.

contentSections.body: Kindness belongs in the framing — system, not people — never in the severity rating itself. A genuine Blocker stays a Blocker; the discipline is describing it without blame-coded language, not describing it as less severe than it is.

Distinguish a finding that only looks complete from one that's genuinely actionable

title: Lab — Write a Complete Audit Report
description: Take findings from earlier in this phase (or fresh ones) and write the complete report around them: summary, method, scope, findings with evidence, severities, and recommendations — the actual document a client would receive.

learningObjectives.text: Structure a complete audit report around how executive and developer readers will actually use it
Write findings, recommendations and an executive summary that are specific, honest and system-framed

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Use findings from an earlier lab in this phase (the evidence pack or the prioritised backlog both work well as source material), or a fresh, smaller set if starting new. This lab produces the actual report document: not a description of what a good report contains, but the real thing.

contentSections.title: Write a complete audit report
contentSections.brief: Using at least 5-6 real findings (from an earlier lab in this phase, or freshly gathered), write a complete audit report: executive summary, methodology and scope, findings section (severity-ordered, consistent format, each with what/where/who/what-to-do), and recommendations.
contentSections.deliverable: A full report: summary, method, scope, findings with evidence, severities and recommendations — structured for how it will actually be used, not the order testing happened.

stages.title: Structure the document and write methodology/scope
stages.instructions: Lay out the report's sections (summary, methodology/scope, findings by severity, appendix). Write the methodology/scope section from an actual scope document if you have one, or state clearly what was and wasn't tested.
stages.checkpoint: The document has a clear section structure, and methodology/scope states exactly what was tested and any exclusions.

stages.title: Write each finding in a consistent format
stages.instructions: For each finding, use the same fields in the same order: title, severity, WCAG citation (where applicable), location, user-impact statement, recommendation. Make sure every recommendation states an outcome and general technique rather than unverified specific code, unless the technique is genuinely near-universal.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has all four required elements (what/where/who/what-to-do) explicit and specific, in a consistent format.

stages.title: Order findings by severity and check the language
stages.instructions: Order the findings section by severity, highest first. Read back through every finding and remove any blame-coded language, reframing onto the system without changing any severity rating or fact.
stages.checkpoint: Findings are severity-ordered, and no finding's language judges a person or team rather than describing the system.

stages.title: Write the executive summary and self-check
stages.instructions: Write the executive summary last, once the findings are final. State the real headline plainly — including any top-severity finding by name — without either inflating or minimising the overall picture. Then run the self-check below.
stages.checkpoint: Every rubric criterion below is met, or you've noted specifically what's still missing.

rubric.criterion: The structure serves both an executive and a developer reader
rubric.meets: An executive could read only the summary and get the real headline; a developer could jump straight to a specific finding without reading the whole document.

rubric.criterion: Every finding has all four elements explicit
rubric.meets: What, where, who, and what-to-do are each a specific, stated sentence — none left implicit or generic.

rubric.criterion: Recommendations describe outcomes, not unverified specific code
rubric.meets: Codebase-dependent fixes are described as an outcome and general technique; only genuinely near-universal techniques are shown as literal code.

rubric.criterion: The executive summary is honest in both directions
rubric.meets: Any top-severity finding is named plainly in the summary itself, and the overall tone matches the real severity distribution — neither inflated nor minimised.

rubric.criterion: Language is system-framed throughout
rubric.meets: No finding's wording judges a person or team's competence or effort — severity ratings stay fully accurate regardless of tone.

contentSections.body: A report you've never actually written end to end is a set of principles you've only read about — this lab is the difference between knowing what a good report contains and having produced the real document.

title: Checkpoint — Writing the Report
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the module before it, and further back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core report-writing distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Writing the Report

questions.prompt: Why should a report's findings be ordered by severity rather than by the order testing happened to occur in?

options.label: Chronological order reflects the auditor's own process, not what an executive or developer reader actually needs first — a genuine blocker could end up buried on page 60
It doesn't actually matter which order findings appear in
Chronological order is required by WCAG

questions.explanation: A structure built around how the report will actually be used — severity-first, consistent format — serves readers far better than one that just reflects the sequence testing happened to occur in.

questions.prompt: What four elements does every finding need stated explicitly?

options.label: What's wrong, where it is, who it affects and how, and what to do about it
A title, a citation, a severity label, and a signature
A screenshot, a video, a transcript, and a citation

questions.explanation: A finding needs what/where/who/what-to-do each stated as its own explicit sentence — a citation and severity label alone don't substitute for any of them.

questions.prompt: 'This affects users with disabilities' is attached identically to every finding in a 60-finding report. What's the problem?

options.label: Being true of every finding equally means it conveys zero information distinguishing this finding's actual impact from any other's
It's factually inaccurate
It should be replaced with a specific medical diagnosis

questions.explanation: A useful impact statement names the specific task, mechanism, and user category — a generic statement that fits every finding equally communicates nothing about any one of them specifically.

questions.prompt: An auditor writes exact class names and DOM structure into a recommendation, without having seen the client's actual codebase. What's the risk?

options.label: The guessed code may not match the real structure at all, which can mislead a developer more than an honest, outcome-focused description would
There's no risk — specific code is always more helpful than a general description
The only risk is that it looks less impressive

questions.explanation: Unverified specific code risks being actively wrong for the real codebase, which can mislead a developer more than an honest description of the needed outcome and general technique.

questions.prompt: An executive summary states '57 of 60 findings were Medium or below' while never mentioning the 3 genuine Blocker findings anywhere in the summary. Every number is accurate. Is this honest?

options.label: No — this is dishonest by omission; foregrounding a reassuring true statistic while omitting the most consequential findings misleads the reader
Yes — every individual stated fact is verifiably true
It can't be judged without knowing the exact WCAG citations

questions.explanation: Individually true facts, selectively arranged, can produce a false overall impression — a summary should represent the real overall picture, and a reader shouldn't be able to finish it without learning the most consequential findings exist.

questions.prompt: Is overstating a genuinely moderate audit's findings with alarmist language ('riddled with severe failures') a safe way to make sure stakeholders take it seriously?

options.label: No — it teaches stakeholders to discount severity language generally, which buries any genuinely severe findings under the same inflated tone as everything else
Yes — more alarming language always gets faster action regardless of accuracy
Yes, as long as the findings section itself uses accurate severity ratings

questions.explanation: Overcorrecting toward alarmism relative to the actual findings teaches stakeholders to discount the auditor's severity language, which undermines trust in the findings that genuinely do warrant urgency.

questions.prompt: 'The developers failed to add alt text... this carelessness affects blind users' and 'the image-upload workflow doesn't currently require alt text as a step' describe the same underlying fact. What's the actual difference?

options.label: One judges the people involved, the other frames the gap as a system/process issue — the second is far less likely to trigger defensiveness that slows down the actual fix
There's no meaningful difference between the two
The second version is less accurate

questions.explanation: Framing on the system rather than on people produces the same facts and the same fix with a dramatically different reception — defensiveness tends to slow down fixes, and it colors how a team reads every subsequent finding in the report too.

questions.prompt: An auditor softens a genuine Blocker rating down to Medium specifically to avoid demoralising the development team. Is this consistent with this module's guidance on kind, system-framed language?

options.label: No — kindness belongs in the framing language, never in the accuracy of the severity rating itself
Yes — softening severity ratings is exactly what system-framed, kind language means
Yes, as long as the finding's description still mentions the real impact somewhere

questions.explanation: This module's guidance is about language, not rating accuracy — a genuine Blocker should stay a Blocker regardless of tone; softening the number to spare feelings misrepresents real impact.

questions.prompt: What are the three explicit inputs to a severity rating?

options.label: Impact, frequency, and whether there's a genuine workaround
WCAG conformance level, citation number, and fix cost
Report length, tester seniority, and client size

questions.explanation: Severity is rated from impact, frequency, and workaround — three separate, explicit questions, independent of WCAG conformance level.

questions.from: 3+ modules back — Evidence That Holds Up
questions.prompt: Why does a screen reader announcement need a verbatim transcript rather than a description like 'it sounded wrong'?

options.label: A verbatim transcript is a specific, checkable claim a fix can be verified against; a vague description of impression can't be verified either way
WCAG requires all announcements to be transcribed word-for-word
There's no real difference between the two

questions.explanation: A verbatim transcript is checkable evidence a developer can compare their fix's output against directly, unlike a vague impression that can't be verified.

contentSections.body: None of these need to be perfect. What matters is which ones needed a guess — that's what the next checkpoint will bring back.
